articles.title: Lawsuits Can’t Restrain Big Tech
articles.author: Rob Larson
articles.content: When the government first filed major antitrust lawsuits targeting Big Tech back in 2020, many people were optimistic that the long-standing practice of public legal action against monopolistic companies could rein in these economy-dominating corporations. But as these pages have covered , this “techlash” has come to little. Antitrust law has conformed to its castrated character of recent decades, with the state unable to bring itself to seriously restrain, let alone break up, the giant companies even after they were ruled to be full monopolies just months before. Recently, when it comes to enforcing the law against the tech giants, new lows have been reached. “Neither Realistic nor Needed” Google’s first antitrust suit concerned its control of web search, and it was ruled to have operated a monopoly yet was given only a slap on the wrist. Rather than being broken up or forced to sell off any of its major corporate units like Chrome, the court imposed rather toothless “behavioral” remedies, barring exclusive default-search deals and requiring the company to share some search data with rivals. A second case was brought by the Department of Justice in 2023 over Google’s “ad tech” business, an industry term referring to the segment of the company’s ad business that helps independent websites (such as news publishers) sell ads on their own pages. Google owns what are by far the dominant tools for this market, including the exchange itself (known as AdX) where advertisers find publishers as well as the servers that deliver the ad content. The company charges a 20 percent fee to run ad auctions for websites, which occur in fractions of a second as your browser opens the webpage in question. It should be said at the outset that ad tech is a small part of Google — the $30 billion in revenue it brought in for 2025 comes to just 7 percent of Alphabet’s total revenue, and that share has been in decline for years. The Justice Department wanted the court to force Google to sell off AdX. The judge’s full opinion remained under seal for weeks while both sides were given the chance to redact confidential information from it. The now-revealed remedies include a requirement for Google to make its ad exchange interoperable with competitors, meaning that using Google’s marketplace for finding bidders wouldn’t lock publishers into using its other tools. It also forces the company to share some real-time bidding data with publishers. But unsurprisingly, in Google’s second monopolist verdict in two years, the company was still not subjected to any form of breakup. Judge Leonie M. Brinkema found such a measure to be “neither realistic nor needed.” Instead she settled for narrower measures such as those mentioned above as well as obliging Google to retain a court-appointed monitor with limited power over the firm. The “remedies” will stay in place for only six years , rather than the fifteen years that the government sought. And Google of course plans to appeal the finding of monopolization, which will take some years. The company is now an adjudicated monopolist twice over, but the liberal state has failed to even partially rewrite Alphabet. Hang Together Meanwhile, the private arm of the techlash appears to be producing more serious consequences. Years of attempts by litigants to sue the platforms for their harmful content have failed, due to strong legal protections shielding the companies for material posted by users. But more recently, users have hit on the legal argument that the designs of the platforms themselves are harmful, and intentionally so. Reporting and disclosures about such design choices have bolstered these cases, from the Wall Street Journal in its damning “Facebook Files” series that drew on leaked internal Meta research to company documents unsealed in court. (An illustrative quote : “Targeting 11 year olds feels like tobacco companies a couple decades ago [and today]. Like we’re seriously saying ‘we have to hook them young’ here.”) These revelations showed that company engineers and executives were quite aware of the addictive properties of now-common social media and online video platforms, including the infinite scroll of social media feeds, the autoplay algorithm of online video sites, and the regular barrage of push notifications that attempt to pull users back to the platforms. Juries are finding for the plaintiffs in these cases, most famously for litigants in Los Angeles and New Mexico, where Meta is supposed to pay out hundreds of millions of dollars in total penalties. In August, Meta reached a major settlement with most of the US state attorneys general, which have sued the company on similar grounds of user harm. That settlement involved both a cash payout and promised changes to Meta’s app designs. The settlement awards up to $18 billion to the forty-eight states, Washington, DC, and three territories taking part in the suit, to be apportioned based on the states’ populations. However, Meta will only pay out 70 percent of this amount unless YouTube and TikTok adopt similar changes and together pay an amount equal to the remaining 30 percent, about $5.3 billion. Even if Meta ends up paying the higher amount, the figure is quite small — according to the corporation’s most recent 10-Q filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, its last quarterly profit was $15.8 billion. So the settlement represents the company’s net income for just three months, but paid out over a decade, and at a time when Meta is firehosing money into a dubious data center build-out. For a payout that settles so much liability, and over two decades of operation, this sum is a wretched pittance. The “behavioral” penalties, rules that the company is now obliged to follow, are also less than inspiring. Facebook and Instagram nominally require users under eighteen to use teen accounts, which are now mandated to include “night mode,” which blocks most app features between midnight and 6 a.m., and “school mode,” which prevents push notifications during school hours; minors will also be limited to two hours of use per day. Unless, of course, teen users can figure out how to circumvent the changes — for example by using their parents’ often-on phones to change the settings and disable these modes. But what teen is more tech savvy than their parents? Nine-Tenths of the Law The public and private legal processes continue to grind along, with a Justice Department case against Apple and a Federal Trade Commission case against Amazon still pending, and Meta continues to deal with thousands of civil lawsuits from individual users and school districts. But so far, neither of these legal routes looks very promising in terms of reining in the power of the Big Tech platforms. What will it take to impose real penalties or constraints on the tech giants? Tech workers are seeking to organize and use their leverage to demand change at the companies from within; meanwhile, politicians like Bernie Sanders have called for taking a 50 percent stake in the major artificial intelligence companies. Seeing the continued failures of the legal strategy to rein in Big Tech, it increasingly looks like we need organized tech workers and a political movement for real regulation and public control — up to and including the socialist solution of nationalization of their pivotal algorithms and networks. For companies that are apparently too big to break up, socialism may succeed where liberal regulatory efforts have failed. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Protests in France
articles.author: Dennis Broe
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Monday after a series of often violent confrontations between high school and university students, pensioners and unions on the one side and police on the other, the foreign press was ablaze with graphic descriptions of “burning cars…and shattered shop windows” as The New York Times photo caption put it over a photo of a “burned-out vehicle.” The Murdoch press was even more graphic with The New York Post claiming the “riots in France” were an “attack on civilisation” led by “Muslim communities.” While Murdoch’s Wall Street Journal lead headline blared that “Rioting Sweeps Country,” then returned to commercial oblivion right next to it with “How Coke Beat Pepsi To Supply Beverages at KFC.” The New York Times’ more “reasonable” approach sounded the alarm as across Europe, following the French, “young people and workers” were tempted by “promises of radical change.” Yes there was violence and some looting but the resort to portraying these demonstrations as a pure eruption of violence is the last resort of a government and a media which has lost control of the narrative. The protests have now moved beyond high school and university students to a reemergence of the rural and periurban (or urban fringe) disenfranchised and pensioners with October 17 marking the convergence of “ le jaune et le jeune, ” the Yellow (Vests) and the Youth. The protests have now spurred the unions as well who will be staging a mass action that may turn into a general strike on November 5th, occasioning even in the mainstream press here in France a description of the moment as “the end of Macronisme,” that is, of nearly a decade of neoliberal “reforms” which his administration has wrought including a vast redistribution of wealth upwards, declining medical and education infrastructure and an increasingly more repressive police presence to squash dissent at these “reforms.” Related: The World Cup, the LA Olympics and the Death of Sports Innocence The government has responded to these protests not with the Five Stages of Grief, but with Three Stages of Control. The first response was to deny their importance, a response that had to be abandoned as the protests grew in strength and frequency and as the claims of a disintegrating education system and lack of promise for the future gained credence with the rest of the society. Then came slight acknowledgement and placating. President Macron has mostly been absent from the political stage during this entire period, since his latest approval rating at 15 percent means he would only be adding flame to the fire. In his place, the Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu proposed adding 3000 substitute teachers to the high school system which was immediately understood for what it was, a measure to stop the demonstrations with the temporary teachers then let go when tensions decreased. The third stage though is open violence on the part of the police, who have arrested 8000 demonstrators, largely minors, in a repression that has been described even in the mainstream press here as “historic in its scale.” The demonstrators know that when they take to the streets they will be met with tear gas and billy clubs and they now know that they must respond in kind, in a pitched battle for control of the streets, defending their right to protest. One of the most common placards in the corteges is “ACAB,” All Cops Are Bastards.” On the 17th, police quickly baracaded the area around the main protest staging ground at Republique, not allowing protestors to enter and, when they tried to surmount the barriers, met with tear gas grenades whizzing over their heads and the young people frantically running in one direction or another to avoid the canisters. Related: Media Watch: The Scandals Behind the Scandals Symbols of “Rioting” gleefully taken up by the press The LFI, France Unbowed, the main party favoring the peaceful part of these protests noted that “Confrontation seems to be the goal of this law enforcement strategy,” accusing the police of having “organized the disorder.” The mainstream media focus on demonstrator’s violence—street violence portrayed as flashy and graphic—is at the expense of the slower and more deadly structural violence that the protestors are attempting to call attention to. The economist Thomas Piketty points out that what Macron has presided over in the area of education is a 20 percent drop in funding per student when adjusted for inflation with teachers’ pay outside the elite universities, which Macron’s polices of entrepreneurship have promoted, falling by 50 percent. This has resulted in universities and high schools with collapsing ceilings, in school facilities with little of no heating or cooling and in administrative offices deserted because of declining salaries. This in a country, as Piketty points out, where in the last decades private wealth has risen from 300 to 600 percent of the total and where, for example, the wealthiest companies grow richer as the oil and gas company TotalEnergies reported an 11.2 billion euro profit this year. Across Europe, as in France, these protests now also constitute a convergence of struggles. In Italy, in another linking of the jaune and the jeune , pro-Palestinian eruptions as well as protests against Meloni’s far-right repression and austerity from students and activists in the North are joined by road haulers, farmers and fishermen in the South whose living is threatened by the high price of energy. Likewise, students in Belgium have taken to the streets as well as in Spain whose squares are being occupied in a protest against tenant expulsions and the high price of rents not only in Madrid but now throughout the country. Yes there was violence on October 17th but part of that violence followed a global pattern of peaceful protest being succeeded, often in the evening after the protests, by gangs of armed hoodlums, with the most notorious of these the Black Block often accused of being police provocateurs. The global pattern of peaceful protests followed by violence also characterised protests against inadequate housing in Hong Kong in 2020 and against corruption in Indonesia in 2025. The violence then allows both the governments and the media to ignore the very real griviences of the protestors and focus instead on what The New York Times always terms “chaos” which for that paper is the inevitable result of any questioning of the bourgeois order. Related: Game of Pedophiles Two stark moments characterise these protests. One is that Le Monde mourned the fact that the Socialist candidate for president Raphaël Glucksmann, who won what that party quaintly terms a “primary” by getting only 70 percent of 144,000 votes, could not visit the protests because he would be booed and laughed off the barricades. This represents not the “ultra-left” position of the protestors but rather their understanding that the centrist parties, even those that call themselves left, represent only a “college-educated elite.” The other symbol mourned in the press was the toppling in Marseille of a statue of Marianne, signifier of the French Revolution. This is not a descent into anarchy. It is a recognition that after four Revolutions in under 75 years—1789, 1830, 1848 and 1871—to finally rid the country of the aristocracy, the bourgeois republic that was installed now no longer represents the interests of the majority of its people. As one protestor put it, “We’re following in the tradition of May ‘68” and in that tradition these protestors will find their own Marianne.

articles.title: Evangelicals’ 10 Lessons in Leader Development for the Left
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content: Last week , I looked at what Rick Warren’s 1995 classic The Purpose Driven Church can teach the Left about recruitment in our atomized era. But getting people through the door is only half the battle. Seeker-sensitive evangelicalism didn’t buck America’s decades-long decline in membership organizations simply by attracting crowds. It couldn’t have grown without systematically turning newcomers into members, members into leaders, and leaders into recruiters. As Warren puts it, “Our ultimate goal at Saddleback is to turn an audience into an army.” This is where the Left is weakest. Radical and progressive organizations generally lose most people we bring in and develop only a fraction of the rest into organizers able and willing to recruit those around them. Survey data shows a dramatic difference between how today’s evangelicals and leftists recruit. Whereas 82 percent of megachurch attendees first heard of their church via a personal invitation from a coworker, friend, or family member, the same was true for only 21 percent of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members. This reliance on media rather than personal invitations is also the norm among progressives in the United States and abroad . What would it take for the Left to turn this around? Many answers can be found in The Purpose Driven Church . More than a collection of organizing tips, it offers a model for how to generate self-reinforcing growth: belonging fosters commitment; commitment opens the door to training; training and responsibility develop leaders; and those leaders bring in new people who repeat the process. In an era when community is far less likely to arise organically from daily life, moving toward a similarly systematic model is indispensable. Of course, leftists’ opponents are more powerful, and our organizations must be more democratic. But if we’re going to move beyond relying on social media and news headlines to recruit self-selecting, college-educated activists, we need to learn how to consistently develop supporters into leaders and recruiters. Warren’s model offers ten lessons for making that shift. 1. Get Smaller to Get Bigger At Saddleback, small groups consist of about a dozen people who meet weekly to collectively study, volunteer, break bread, and lend support to each other. They meet in homes because homes are free, relaxed, quicker to get to in sprawled-out Orange County, and “infinitely expandable.” Volunteer leaders run the small groups, with trained lay pastors overseeing group clusters. Warren warns that when church is all lecture (“Sit still while I instill”), people can attend for a year without making a friend. He urges including some relational activity in every gathering and swears by weekend retreats: “The amount of time a person spends with other members at a single forty-eight-hour retreat is greater than the time they will spend together on Sundays over a year.” Behind all this is a simple finding about why people stay. As Warren writes, “Relationships are the glue that holds a church together.” National surveys find that about 40–60 percent of megachurch Sunday attendees participate in at least one small group. Apart from strong union organizing committees, most of our organizations have no equivalent to evangelicals’ weekly small groups or the Belgian Workers’ Party’s analogous groupes de base . 2. Build a Robust Ladder of Commitment Warren explains that people sit at different levels of commitment and that an organization’s job is to move them up the ladder, step by step. Saddleback pictured this as five concentric circles, with the following mid-1990s figures: •Community: 31,000 people who had visited at least four times in a year •Crowd: 10,000 regular weekend attenders •Congregation: 5,000 official members •Committed: 3,500 members who had signed a covenant to pray daily, tithe, and join a small group •Core: 1,500 lay ministers who ran the church’s work The point is to systematically move them inward. “A crowd is not a church — but a crowd can be turned into a church,” he writes. And the process doesn’t end at the center: “What happens when people finally get to the core? We move them back out into the community for ministry!” To make the ladder concrete, Saddleback used a baseball diamond. At each base, newcomers completed a class and signed a covenant: membership (101), maturity (201), ministry (301), and evangelism (401). In most churches, members stall halfway around. To avoid this, Warren insists that the organization, not just the newcomer, is responsible for making the climb happen. “Many churches mistakenly assume that once a person has received Christ, the sale has been consummated, and it is now up to the new believer to follow through with his commitment and join the church. This is nonsense.” Instead, “It is the church’s responsibility to take the initiative in assimilating new people into the congregation.” Many progressive and leftist chapters have some form of ladder of engagement, but few groups have made it anywhere near as visible and systematic as Saddleback. Too often, the ladder collapses into two rungs: a mass event (a rally, a canvass shift, an email list) and a small, burnt-out staff or volunteer cadre who do everything else, with few clearly laid-out steps in between. As exciting as it is that DSA is now 130,000 strong, we shouldn’t overlook the fact that roughly two-thirds of members who joined during our first big surge after 2016 left within five years, and that almost half of all former members left after just one year. As was explained earlier this year in Democratic Left , “overall, member retention rates are basically unchanged since 2020.” Imagine, instead, a clear path from event attendee to dues-paying member to small-group member to trained organizer who recruits others, with a short class and a clear commitment at each step. And not just in big electoral campaigns, but year-round. 3. Instill Ideology via Organizing Megachurches are often dismissed as superficial spectacles consisting of little more than charismatic preachers, self-help fluff, and smart marketing techniques. That’s true enough for some fringe Prosperity Gospel–type churches, but such a critique misses the mark when it comes to Warren’s theory or Saddleback’s practice . Community and appealing services help get people in the door, but ideology is also indispensable to the model, especially because it inspires the conviction needed to sustain members’ commitment. “No one stays with a difficult task unless they are convinced there is a good reason for doing so,” he notes. During Saddleback’s early years, when volunteers had to set up and tear down everything each Sunday, Warren found himself exhausted, lugging equipment after half the crew failed to show. His lesson: “You must know why you do what you do or else you’ll be defeated by discouragement.” But Warren didn’t rely on sermons to spread conviction. “Conviction is contagious: People acquire it by being around other people who have it.” Proximity to conviction, Warren notes, is a major reason Saddleback emphasizes small groups. Nor does Warren think recruitment can depend on big ideas alone; immediate needs are normally the main motivating factor: “While most unbelievers aren’t looking for truth, they are looking for relief. This gives us the opportunity to interest them in truth.” Once people were inside, Saddleback emphasized systematic ideological education, offering nine-month Bible study courses and a theology course covering twelve foundational Christian doctrines, taught twice weekly over twenty-seven weeks. Progressive activists feel strongly about many issues but often lack an overarching way to make sense of the world and give meaning to individuals’ efforts within it. Socialists do have such an ideology — and a mass membership organization through which to cultivate it. But unlike the relatively small, self-selecting, college-educated layer currently drawn to DSA and progressive causes, most people won’t be attracted by ideas alone. As with churches, the initial draw for millions of working people will be relief from immediate problems. Once people join an organization, form relationships, and take on meaningful responsibilities, their convictions and views can deepen. Yet too many liberals and radicals remain captive to a particularly college-educated faith in the transformative power of ideas alone. Organizing normally requires a different sequence: bringing people together around immediate needs, deepening their convictions through participation, and helping them expand their understanding through collective study. 4. Ask for Big Commitments Many activists assume that asking too much will scare people off, but Warren argues the opposite is often the case. “I’ve discovered that challenging people to a serious commitment actually attracts people rather than repels them,” he writes. The reason is that people are hungry for meaning: “Many unbelievers are fed up and bored with what the world offers. They are looking for something greater than themselves, something worth giving their lives to.” Not everybody can make big commitments; some will stay in the crowd, and that’s fine. But if you don’t regularly make big asks, you don’t provide others with the opportunity to step up. Apart from a few fringe sects, most American Left and progressive organizations set a low bar for formal entry (though their insider culture often undermines mass recruitment and retention) but rarely help members take on more. Warren’s approach shows how to pair big asks with manageable steps. Saddleback’s maturity covenant, renewed annually, asked for three concrete habits (a daily devotional time, a tithe of 10 percent of income, and weekly small-group attendance), and members carried laminated covenant cards in their wallets. This approach has financial implications. Whereas the vast majority of the nonprofit industrial complex is funded by wealthy foundations, 91 percent of the annual income of megachurches comes from tithes and dues. If your organization can’t rely on self-funding from below, that should raise major red flags about whether you are building meaningful stakes and ownership. Warren observes that membership in many organizations and churches today is thin to the point of being almost meaningless. He tells of preaching at one church that “had over a thousand members on its roll but had less than two hundred people attending services! What is the value of having that kind of membership?” Saddleback took the opposite approach. To join, you had to take Class 101, a four-hour class taught in a single day, with a quiz at the end on the church’s purposes. Then you signed a membership covenant, which included a pledge to invite the unchurched and to welcome visitors. Warren explains the logic: “I believe the most important class in a church is the membership class because it sets the tone and expectation level for everything else that follows. The very best time to elicit a strong commitment from your members is at the moment they join. If little is required to join, very little can be expected from your members later on.” Membership also came with warmth. For years, Warren and his wife hosted a monthly “Pastor’s Chat” for new members and visitors in their home, and older members paid for the meals at quarterly banquets for new members. His test of whether assimilation is working is a nice one for any organization: “The community talks about ‘that church,’ the crowd talks about ‘this church,’ but the congregation talks about ‘our church.’ Members have a sense of ownership. They are contributors, not just consumers.” Warren cites a Gallup finding that only 10 percent of church members were active in any ministry (i.e., volunteering within the church or through its community service). He adds that the “encouraging news that Gallup uncovered is this: 40 percent of all members have expressed an interest in having a ministry, but they have never been asked or they don’t know how. This group is an untapped gold mine!” Warren learned this the hard way. In Saddleback’s early years, he and his wife Kay did nearly everything: setting up, taking down, printing bulletins, cleaning bathrooms, storing equipment in their garage. After a few years, he was burning out. So, at a midweek service, he confessed that he couldn’t do it all and offered the congregation a trade. “I’ll make you a deal. If you agree to do the ministry of this church, I’ll make sure you’re well fed!” Delegating responsibility worked. “After making this decision, Saddleback exploded with growth.” Today, 30 percent of megachurch members volunteer regularly. Once people step up, trust them. “At Saddleback, the implementers are the decision makers. The people who do the ministry get to make their own decisions about that ministry. We do not separate authority from responsibility, but trust people with both.” His favorite example: “One time a woman came to me and said, ‘We need a prayer ministry.’ I said, ‘I agree! You’re it!’” She asked whether she needed to be elected or approved first. He told her to just announce a meeting in the bulletin and start it. As he puts it, “You bring out the best in people by giving them a challenge, giving them control, and giving them the credit.” Delegation and decision-making are trickier in democratic unions and political organizations, where individual initiative should remain consistent with agreed-upon goals. But within that framework, scaling up depends largely on empowering members to take on work and leadership responsibilities. As with all the lessons laid out here, we should experiment and see what works. 5. Treat Organizing as a Skill Warren rejects the idea that dedication is enough to grow, writing that “it takes more than dedication to lead a church to grow; it takes skill.” He even goes after prayer: “Somebody needs to boldly state the obvious: Prayer alone will not grow a church. Some of the greatest prayer warriors I know are pastors and members of dying churches.” So Saddleback trained people constantly. Members attended one-day Life Skills Seminars covering specific skills, including how to get along with other people. “People must be taught how to develop relationships. Although this seems obvious, very few churches take time to teach their members how to relate to each other.” And Warren warns leaders never to demand something without showing people how to do it: “Exhortation without explanation leads to frustration.” The Left has its own versions of “just pray harder.” One is “just stick with it, things will eventually turn around.” Another is “just have the right politics.” Dedication matters, and organizational solutions can’t solve bad politics. But especially in our hyperatomized society, organizing is a skill that must be learned, and even building relationships requires deliberate cultivation. The best unions already treat organizing this way, with regular trainings and mentoring that follow a learn-one, do-one, teach-one model. But beyond such progressive pockets, sustained training is rare. It’s hard to see how the Left could recruit widely beyond self-selecting college-educated radicals until we give our members the skills and confidence to actively recruit their neighbors and until we make our organizations more welcoming, as laid out in part one of this series and in the work of Hahrie Han . A 2021 national survey shows that over 80 percent of DSA members have a bachelor’s degree or higher — compared with 44 percent of nondenominational evangelicals . 6. Focus on External Work “Jesus did not say, ‘I have come that you might have meetings.’” Warren argues that the average church would be healthier if it cut half its meetings, since “[o]ne of the reasons church members don’t witness to their neighbors is because they don’t know them! They are always at church, attending meetings.” People’s time is scarce. So if a member offered four hours a week, “the last thing I would do would be to put him on some committee.” Saddleback had no committees at all, relying instead on seventy-nine lay ministries. “Committees discuss it, but ministries do it.” Warren also notes who complains the most: “In a war, you always find the highest morale and sense of camaraderie among those serving on the front line. . . . The biggest complainers in any church are usually committee members with nothing else to do.” Milwaukee’s “sewer socialist” leader Victor Berger made the same observation a century ago: “when people are constantly absorbed in doing things, and in preparing for still greater things, the petty jealousies and small causes for strife and dissension disappear.” Leftists should try to focus as much of our energy as possible on external work, not interminable factionalism and internal bureaucracy. Focusing outward, however, is challenging not just because democratic deliberation is essential, but because many of us prefer talking to each other, which is more comfortable than going out and trying to win over skeptics. 7. Combat Individualism Warren is blunt about the cultural enemy: “Our culture’s preoccupation with individualism and independence must be replaced with the biblical concepts of interdependence and mutuality.” And he admits that changing this is hard: “Believe me, it is an incredibly difficult task to lead people from self-centered consumerism to being servant-hearted Christians.” Warren defines fellowship as mutual obligation: “In our church we define koinonia (fellowship) as ‘being as committed to each other as we are to Jesus Christ.’” Leftist theory agrees that none of us are islands. But too often, we don’t build that belief into our culture. Instead, we often reproduce individualism by focusing on online posting and self-expression over pragmatically building collective power. Putting organization and collective goals ahead of individual egos and moral self-satisfaction should become our cultural norm. 8. Put Your Money Where Your Mission Is “The way we spend our time and the way we spend our money show what is really important to us, regardless of what we claim to believe,” writes Warren. This principle was evident from the start: before Saddleback’s first service, members of his tiny Bible study went about $6,500 into debt on their personal credit cards to pay for outreach. Warren describes the spending as an investment and warns that “[w]hen finances get tight in a church, often the first thing cut is the evangelism and advertising budget. That is the last thing you should cut. It is the source of new blood and life for your church.” On the Left, how much money goes to reaching new people, and how much goes to maintaining existing operations? Solid numbers are hard to come by, but my impression is that only a tiny sliver of nonprofit and progressive funding goes toward external growth. And the labor movement certainly fails this test badly. Unions are sitting on over $35 billion in assets, yet most spend only a small share of their budgets on organizing the unorganized. 9. Develop Strong Leaders Warren is a big believer in strong leadership. “The most critical factor in a new ministry isn’t the idea, but the leadership,” he writes. In 1979, as a seminary student, he surveyed the hundred largest churches in America and found that many had long-serving pastors. For Warren, the lesson was that leadership continuity allows people to build the trust and relationships needed for lasting growth. But he also emphasizes that “healthy churches are built on a process, not on personalities.” Much of the Left is still averse to leadership, or at least to strong leaders. That’s a mistake. We need to identify, develop, and empower people with the experience and skills to guide large numbers of people through struggle. And one of the most important tasks of strong leaders is to develop new leaders at all levels. Of course, there are dangers: leaders can ossify or become detached from the membership. But the answer is robust democratic accountability, not a culture of horizontalism or musical chairs at the top. 10. Test, Measure, and Adjust Warren’s most important lesson may be his method. Saddleback treated retention and development with the same experimental spirit it applied to recruitment. Every month, the staff reviewed a six-page “Saddleback Snapshot” tracking how many people sat on each rung of the ladder. “The Snapshot forces us to take an honest look each month at how well our church is fulfilling its purposes. Bottlenecks in the system become easy to spot.” Saddleback also ran three continuous feedback loops: first-impression cards from visitors, feedback cards from regular attenders (processing them took two full-time secretaries and a dozen volunteers), and staff evaluation sheets covering everything from parking to the sermon. Warren compares this to National Football League players reviewing game film every Monday. “Growing churches should always be asking, ‘How can we do it better?’ They are ruthless in evaluating their services and ministries.” He’s equally skeptical of easy success stories. “Anytime you hear a pastor attribute the growth of his church to one single factor, realize that he is either oversimplifying what has occurred, or he may not be recognizing the real reason his church is growing.” Saddleback was also part of a much larger ecosystem of learning. The Church Growth Movement, built on the research of Donald McGavran and others, spent decades studying what made congregations grow or die. Over the years, countless pastors have compared notes at seminars, and hundreds of reports have been published detailing what’s working and what’s not. Beyond exchanging lessons, evangelical networks and denominations raised funds, trained organizers, and provided seed funding to launch new churches and initiatives. In Left organizations, by contrast, we tend to cherry-pick our wins, blame our losses on external factors, avoid honest postmortems, and stick with siloed routines instead of scaling up successful initiatives. If we want to build durable mass organizations, that should change. Our Challenge None of this means copying evangelical churches wholesale. Not every practice will work for us, especially since Left organizations should operate democratically and confront oligarchic power. Rebuilding connection and purpose in atomized America ultimately requires challenging big business, whose increased dominance over our workplaces, our neighborhoods, and our political system has left us alienated and alone. But taking on that power requires structures that can do more than recruit the already convinced: they must build lasting relationships among disconnected people, develop them into organizers, and equip them to recruit and lead others. Three decades ago, evangelicals figured out how to build community in a disconnected society. Our challenge is to turn community-building into the collective power to change society itself. articles.title: Trump Denied Project 2025
articles.author: Ted Vaill
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. By February, 2026, 53% of the goals of “Project 2025” had been initiated or accomplished by Trump and his gang, or 283 out of 532 recommended actions in this Heritage Foundation document that Trump claimed he had nothing to do with. However, the key authors of this document comprised 70% of Trump’s cabinet members, and over 50 of Trump’s senior government officials had direct ties to Project 2025. Over 140 of Trump appointees helped write Project 2025, including Russ Vought, director of Trump’s Office of Management and Budget, Steve Miller, his Deputy Chief of Staff, and Brendon Carr, head of the FCC. Other authors include Rick Dearborn, Christopher Miller, Ken Cuccinelli, Dr. Ben Carson, Peter Navarro, and Edwin Feulner, the co-founder and former President of the Heritage Foundation . The Heritage Foundation was formed in 1973, and became a leading conservative think tank. In recent years, it has shifted its positions on a number issues. They now support: opposing aid to Ukraine, embracing “Trumpism”, doubting election results, supporting significant reductions in the federal workforce and weakening career civil servants’ influence, avoring the U.S. retreating from international foreign policy alignments, opposing “Communists” and “Socialists” in government, *admiring some of the tactics of Joe McCarthy, and*supporting the unitary executive theory. Related: Are We On the Verge of a Revolution? The “unitary executive theory”, championed by Edwin Feulner, Steve Bannon and Steve Miller, lays out a blueprint for an unprecedented expansion of executive powers and “deconstruction of the administrative state”, as Bannon calls it. In 2019, Trump declared that “I have the right to do whatever I want as President”. The theory posits that the President should have sole control over the executive branch. However, past experience in Hungary, Poland and Turkey have shown how centralizing executive power can undermine the rule of law, skew election results, and shrink dissent, increasing the decline of democracy. Implemented Project 2025 objectives by Trump and his cronies have already centralized executive authority and reduced regulatory oversight and undermined our democracy. A past example: the George W. Bush deregulation led up to the 2008 financial crisis, which emboldened corporate misconduct leading to financial abuses and market failures. In the future, the failure to regulate AI could lead to the destruction of civilization. Trump wants the AI industry to control itself, not the government. Related: Time's Up? What to do? Trump has started an unpopular war with Iran, imposed unwise tariffs, and increased by a lot the cost of living for Americans, and he does not care, as he lives in his self- promoting bubble. He looks unwell, and may be inflicted with the dementia that killed his father. Many of the polls show that on November 3 there will be a gigantic blue wave that will return the Democrats to power in the House and Senate. However, if this fails to happen, or if Trump attempts a 1/6-type coup by messing with the Midterms, the only response would be to capitulate to a Trump autocracy or have a civil war. Trump and his billionaires are throwing millions at the Midterm elections to convince voters that the Republicans should stay in power in Congress and throughout the country. If the American voters buy into this Trump and GOP bullshit, all is lost. We will have two more years of Trump’s unitary executive power, and the likely end of our democracy.

articles.title: California Prop 45
articles.author: Aaron Miguel Cantú
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Big Tech companies and California’s largest oil and gas well operator are spending millions to pass a ballot measure that would clear hurdles for industrial projects such as gas pipelines and possibly data centers. Proposition 45 would alter the California Environmental Quality Act, known as CEQA, which requires often time-consuming reviews and public input for infrastructure and other construction projects. Those requirements would be clipped if voters pass the proposition in November, making projects harder to stop or delay. The half-century-old environmental law has come under scrutiny for slowing housing construction, among other complaints. Last year, the state Legislature passed and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bills exempting housing in developed urban and suburban areas from the law and giving “ advanced manufacturing ” businesses a pass. It wasn’t enough to speed along needed housing, clean energy and other projects, say the proposition’s backers. California needs Proposition 45 to further “cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays,” as the measure’s text puts it, and make the state more affordable. But the initiative’s opponents say such appeals are disingenuous. Housing and clean energy have never been “the real agenda behind this ballot measure,” said Woody Little, a spokesperson for the No on Prop 45 campaign. “It’s always been about polluting projects they can get through under the guise of addressing the housing crisis.” In addition to speeding up environmental reviews for housing, wastewater treatment plants and other facilities, the proposition would benefit businesses behind projects that capture climate-warming carbon dioxide pollution. Among them is California Resources Corp., an oil company that has spent $1 million to promote Proposition 45. The firm owns thousands of oil wells in the state and is developing technology it says is capturing carbon dioxide from its Elk Hills natural-gas power plant in Kern County. The proposition excludes new oil and gas production from its provisions but includes carbon dioxide pipelines. A network of political insiders and oil lobbyists has secured state incentives for carbon capture technology, mirroring industry efforts worldwide . California’s anti-emissions plans for the next two decades lean heavily on transporting carbon dioxide, a volatile gas, through hundreds of miles of pipelines spanning urban and rural areas to be buried under the Central Valley. Yet as a solution for climate change, capturing carbon has failed at scale and will likely never succeed , an investigation by the nonprofit newsroom ProPublica found. Related: Environmental Racism in the Shadow of the Port of Los Angeles California Resources Corp. has expanded its political influence in recent years. It is lobbying the state Public Utilities Commission to apply clean-power funds to electricity generated from methane, a fossil fuel, if the exhaust is captured. It’s spending money on state legislative races, funding more than a dozen business-friendly Democrats known to stonewall environmental legislation. And it gave gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, also a Democrat, more than any other politician this election cycle, contributing half a million dollars to his campaign in May. Yet California Resources Corp.’s greatest spending during this election cycle has been devoted to Proposition 45. In December, a company subsidiary gave $500,000 to a committee of the California Chamber of Commerce, the initiative’s sponsor. (The Chamber now brands itself as CalChamber.) In August, California Resources Corp. gave another $500,000 directly to the Yes on 45 campaign. The oil company may have played a role in other contributions to the campaign. A Chamber of Commerce committee lent $2 million to the Proposition 45 campaign in June. The chamber’s board of directors, which includes California Resources Corp. chief executive Francisco Leon, controls that spending. Unlike carbon capture, AI data centers may or may not be expedited by Proposition 45. While the initiative applies to “essential broadband internet access” infrastructure, supporters and opponents of the measure disagree on what this means. But campaign records show companies with data center interests back the proposition. That includes California Resources Corp., which partnered with the developer Beacon Data Centers to advance a 275-megawatt campus for the technology using electricity from its Elk Hills plant. Another company in the sector, Prologis, donated $500,000 for Proposition 45 via its Modern Infrastructure Alliance Action Fund. The company — whose Western regional president, Megan Creecy-Herman, is a Chamber of Commerce board member — is planning five data centers in San Jose. The Modern Infrastructure Alliance Action Fund’s disclosure form lists the law firm Nielsen Merksamer, which formed fake consumer groups to buy ads opposing oil refinery regulation in 2023, the San Francisco Chronicle found. Related: Toxic Smoke, Corporate Power and Neglect in Boyle Heights One Nielsen Merksamer partner, Kurt Oneto, describes himself as the “official proponent” of Proposition 45 and is also a member of the chamber’s board. A law firm representative didn’t return Capital & Main’s call seeking comment. Other data center developers and AI boosters, including Google co-founder and centibillionaire Sergey Brin, spent $10 million through a committee called Building a Better California in support of Proposition 45. Nielsen Merksamer’s phone number is listed as a contact for that committee. Utilities that could benefit from faster approvals for transmission and distribution infrastructure, as well as methane gas capture projects , also gave millions in support of Proposition 45. Pacific Gas & Electric Co., which is developing mixed-use residential and data center projects in San Jose, gave $2.3 million to Yes on 45 through another committee managed by Nielsen Merksamer . Edison International gave $2 million directly to Yes on 45, and its affiliate Southern California Edison Company sent another $2 million to CalChamber’s Business PAC. That committee donated $3.4 million to Yes on 45. Sempra, whose companies include Southern California Gas Company and San Diego Gas & Electric, contributed $1 million to the California Building Industry Association Issues Committee Supporting Proposition 45. More big spending is on the horizon in the final weeks before the midterm. In September, a committee backed by California Resources Corp., Chevron and other corporations, called Californians for Jobs and a Strong Economy, sent $500,000 to a new committee called Golden State Forward. The group’s registration form shows its officers include lawyers at Nielsen Merksamer. At publication time, its main beneficiaries were Assembly candidates Eric Lucan in the Bay Area and David Penaloza in Orange County, both Democrats fending off more progressive challengers in tight races. articles.title: Ford Plant Health Clinic Providers Vote to Join UAW
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: The nurses and providers who care for our members at Ford plants across the country are now joining UAW themselves. On October 20 th , the three registered nurses at the Chicago Stamping Plant voted unanimously for their union in an NLRB election. The previous day, the physician assistant at Kansas City Assembly voted in a self-determination election to be a part of the nurses bargaining unit at Kansas City. They are the first physician assistant to be added to the Ford Salaried Agreement. Plant nurses are also salaried employees. In April of this year, the nurses at Ford Chicago Assembly plant started this momentum by voting to join the UAW. “I’m excited to welcome the nurses at the Chicago Stamping Plant to the UAW,” Region 4 Director Lucas DeSpain said. “They work for Ford too, and they deserve the ability to protect their rights and interests just like their coworkers on the line do.” “The nurses, physician assistants, and other health care providers at Ford plants play a vital role in keeping our members healthy and safe at work. We are honored to have them join our union. We look forward to protecting their rights and ensuring they are also treated fairly by Ford,” said UAW Vice President Laura Dickerson, Ford Department Director . “Ford plant clinic workers are welcome in the UAW, and we encourage them to join us.”

articles.title: Israel and the Sports Boycott
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The stadium is empty but Israel is still in the game. Though any form of isolation of those responsible for genocide is welcome, the growing movement for a sporting boycott of Israel has yet to translate solidarity into meaningful isolation. Two recent developments illustrate this. The first was the decision by Alkmaar, a Dutch city north of Amsterdam, to bar visiting supporters of Israeli football club Hapoel Be’er Sheva from attending its October 15 Europa League match against AZ Alkmaar at the AFAS Stadium. This move followed the violence surrounding the November 2024 Ajax-Maccabi Tel Aviv match in Amsterdam, when Israeli supporters were filmed chanting racist slogans, tearing down Palestinian flags and confronting local residents. Related: Beyond Israeli Apartheid: Why Britain's Greens Are Challenging Zionism Itself Such behavior is hardly unfamiliar among sections of Israeli football supporters, whose racist chants against Palestinians have included the notorious “Death to Arabs” and “Burn down your village.” During last year’s violence in Amsterdam, Maccabi Tel Aviv supporters were also filmed chanting that there were “no children” left in Gaza. These expressions of racism are increasingly encountering resistance from international audiences, many of whom no longer accept Israel’s carefully cultivated image of democracy, civilization and moral exceptionalism. The genocide in Gaza has shattered those illusions. But Israeli supporters are also confronting another reality: growing isolation and the realization that their presence is increasingly unwelcome in sporting spaces they once took for granted. Rather than prompting introspection, such resentment is manifesting itself in further hostility, confrontation and racist abuse. Ramzy Baroud: Left Coast Forum (49:29) The second development came on Oct. 4, when Ireland’s UEFA Nations League fixture against Israel was relocated to Serbia and played behind closed doors. The Football Association of Ireland cited operational and security concerns. But the writing is on the wall: the growing solidarity movement in Ireland has made clear its opposition to sporting engagement with a team representing a state responsible for the genocide in Gaza. Combined with recurring demonstrations at international sporting events involving Israeli teams, Palestinian flags raised by supportive crowds and growing demands for Israel’s exclusion from international competitions, these developments suggest that sport is becoming an increasingly important arena for solidarity and boycott. However, the question remains: Is any of this enough? The answer may lie in the South African experience, where sporting solidarity eventually evolved into a comprehensive international boycott. Related: How Palestinians Face Down the Israeli Genocide: Ramzy Baroud’s Call for Resistance and Solidarity International campaigns to boycott apartheid South Africa began gaining momentum in the 1950s, gradually spreading across academic, activist and political circles. The organized sports boycott began taking shape in earnest in 1959, with the establishment of the South African Sports Association, and soon became a defining feature of the broader boycott movement. The conventional wisdom has since been that white South African society only truly felt the weight of international isolation when the sports boycott took hold. This argument is valid but some important nuances must be understood. Years of intellectual and political groundwork were essential to expand the activist base and build the networks that eventually made the sports boycott possible. In other words, the groundwork preceding the sports boycott was indispensable. Without it, South Africa might never have been excluded from the 1964 Olympic Games and ultimately expelled from the Olympic movement in 1970. One can confidently argue that Palestinians have already established the foundations necessary to make their boycott movement truly global, expanding as it has beyond academic circles into other popular arenas. Related: Israel Is Losing Hollywood But South Africa’s anti-apartheid movement had an advantage that Palestinians have yet to secure. In 1976, more than 20 African countries boycotted the Montreal Olympics over New Zealand’s sporting relationship with apartheid South Africa. This was followed a year later by the Gleneagles Agreement, through which Commonwealth governments committed themselves to discouraging sporting contacts with South Africa. Over time, the boycott tightened its grip, leaving apartheid South Africa increasingly isolated from the international sporting community. Considering that what is taking place in Palestine goes beyond apartheid into genocide, one can argue that the international sporting response remains far below the level of solidarity extended to those living under apartheid in South Africa. Countries supporting Palestine have not declared a comparable collective boycott of sporting events involving Israel, nor have they barred countries supporting Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Israeli teams continue to compete, facing the consequences of popular anger rather than coordinated action by governments and international sporting bodies to hold Israel accountable. While pressure must continue to mount on FIFA, UEFA and the International Olympic Committee, among other sporting institutions, one must remain realistic: these powerful, profit-generating bodies are unlikely to make moral choices unless sustained pressure compels them to do so. Individual athletes, however, have already demonstrated the moral courage that these institutions lack, often placing their convictions above personal gain, fame and even their careers. Related: Iran War Exposing Limits of U.S. Power Among them is Algerian judoka Fethi Nourine, who received a 10-year suspension after withdrawing from the Tokyo Olympics rather than risk facing an Israeli opponent. Sudan’s Mohamed Abdalrasool also refused to compete against the same Israeli opponent, withdrawing from his scheduled Olympic bout. Equally deserving of recognition is Irish goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, who refused to participate in the recent Nations League fixtures against Israel. “My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong,” he declared. But the truth remains: with or without spectators, as long as Israel is allowed to compete, the apartheid state will continue finding its way back into the international sporting community — without accountability and without even ending the ongoing genocide in Gaza. articles.title: The Creativity Con Ate the Middle Class
articles.author: Thomas Frank
articles.content: The faiths and hopes of the postwar middle-class society have mostly evaporated today. Our parents’ beliefs in consensus and the goodness of American civilization have joined mainline Protestantism and the benevolent corporation on some nostalgia channel of discarded ideas. One signature ideal of that era has survived, however. Indeed, it thrives; it glows with an incandescence that time cannot dim. I am referring to our ongoing fascination with creativity, the human power that our affluent-society ancestors liked to believe made life worth living and that was, at the same time, responsible for the forward motion of civilization itself. Every year brings a bumper crop of sunny new literature on this tired old subject. Self-help books tell us how to sharpen our skills and be more creative; Substack writers explore the fascinating details of mental performance; South by Southwest (SXSW) and its many imitators bring together practitioners of this colorful art; governments zone urban areas for innovative pursuits; foundations issue sumptuous prizes to the exceptionally creative; executives from industries like advertising and defense assure us of their dedication to the human imagination; and Silicon Valley sells artificial intelligence as a creativity force multiplier — or, rather, it did before we started to fear AI as a creativity poison that would blunt our mental skills if not obsolete them altogether. The long-running appeal of creativity to middle-class Americans is easy to understand: it is an explanation for progress that seems to put them in history’s starring role. The reason our country is so successful, it assures us, is the day-to-day innovativeness of millions of ordinary but ingenious people. But the actual, real-world effects of creativity have been anything but healthy for the middle-class society. At every step in the long march to our current state of crushing plutocratic inequality, creativity’s holy name was invoked. The big tax cuts of the 1970s and ’80s were done in order to reinvigorate our creativity. Our leaders deregulated banks, did endless favors for tech and pharma, allowed deindustrialization to rust out the heartland, and ushered us generally into a “postindustrial” era in which working people lost their claim on middle-class prosperity — all in order to augment our powers of creativity and innovation. Creativity beguiles us because it dangles before us a beautiful synergy. “The Lamp That Lit the World Can Light Your Life,” declared the first chapter of one of the first big creativity self-help books (published in 1948), and what it meant was that the mental faculty that gave the world its thrilling art and music . . . the mental faculty that made America productive and prosperous above all nations . . . this same mental faculty would also make your humble, everyday life more vivid, more remunerative, more spiritually satisfying, even. Creativity would make you a better worker and a better person at the same time. It was an irresistibly appealing idea. Unlike high-IQ brainpower, which is not accessible to most of us, creativity was supposed to be an almost universal faculty, a thing that everyone could access if they tried hard enough and read the right self-help book. Creativity is thus a democratic vision of human inequality, if such a thing is possible — “democratic yet elitist,” as the historian Samuel Franklin put it in his brilliant 2023 book, The Cult of Creativity . With a little work and a little guidance from experts on the imagination, it was said, we could all claim a personal chunk of the ineffable power wielded by Albert Einstein and Pablo Picasso: a life of prosperity and joy as we studied the great business tycoons and learned to think like artists. Of course, some people always turned out to be more creative than others. Everyone had some helping of the newly discovered ability, yes, but the literature focused almost entirely on the creative potential found in the highly educated people at society’s upper reaches: executives, not line workers; military officers, not enlisted personnel; professionals, not the people who followed their prescriptions. Creativity was about human excellence, about individuals who succeeded — this is who we were to mimic, and this is who we were to become. Creativity eventually became a project for government as well as for individuals, the central idea in a sweeping social vision that is espoused today by educators, tycoons, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and presidents. What sparked the idea’s leap was the launch of Sputnik in 1957, a Soviet triumph that deeply shocked an America that had taken its technological superiority as a matter of faith. Instead of hunting for traitors in physics labs and the State Department, as we had done earlier in the Cold War, the country chose to look inward this time. What Sputnik revealed, commentators concluded, was a national failure of the imagination . A chorus of Jeremiahs scolded us for having grown conformist and apathetic, beguiled by suburban homes and tail-finned cars. Thanks to our long, relaxing bath in the “easy artificiality” of affluence, warned the president of Yale University in 1958, “the fine edge of our faith has been dulled, our creative powers atrophied.” What we required, wrote two-time Democratic presidential candidate Adlai Stevenson, were “innovators, not organization men.” We needed “Creativity for Survival,” as a 1958 magazine headline put it. We had to celebrate nonconformity if America was to prevail. The Sputnik -induced panic over insufficient creativity eventually morphed into one of those grand theories of Progress and the American Character of which our ancestors were so fond. Creativity, the experts declared, was a sort of precious raw material desperately required by complex technological societies like ours. Change was accelerating, blue-collar workers were in decline, and creativity at the top was the thing that would keep our corporations from becoming sterile and stagnant in capitalism’s ceaseless gale. Before too many years had passed, this theory had a name: the “postindustrial society.” America was now said to be a country in which “innovation,” creativity’s twin sibling and our national superpower, drove a kind of economic growth that would soon propel us far beyond the rest of the world. Middle-class culture was saturated with creativity thought in those days. Education commentators pleaded for creative kids who didn’t fit in. Advertising executives began a “creative revolution,” selling cars and soda pops to help us smash the bonds of convention. Creativity was prized by student protesters of the era and also by the university presidents whose offices they occupied. Psychedelic drugs were said to be devices for instant creative enlightenment, and the young people who took them were reported to be exploring ultracreative forms of liberated consciousness. It was an Age of Aquarius for middle-class Americans in their dawning postindustrial society. It was a world of enchantment and magic; of sprawling universities and national research labs; of nuclear power and supercomputers — each of them a testament to the great but unknowable life force of creativity. War and protest are what we remember the ’60s for today, but at the time it seemed like the beginning of a golden age, with moonshots and soaring modernist architecture and science enthroned in its majesty. At the 1964 New York World’s Fair, we rode the Carousel of Progress and marveled at the gifts given to society by the educated and the enlightened — and given by America to the world. And then, it all seemed to go wrong. Military failure in Vietnam, gross corruption in Washington, the oil shock and the energy crisis, epidemic drug use, an economic recession concurrent with inflation — these were crushing blows to Americans’ understanding of themselves. On top of it all was the growing sense that the progress machine had run out of gas. Here is the first sentence of a Washington Post story from November 1978: “It is hardly a matter of doubt anymore: America’s ability to innovate just isn’t what it used to be.” And here is the headline of a different Post essay on the same subject: “Something’s Happened to Yankee Ingenuity.” The alarm was not misplaced. US economic growth had slowed. A trade deficit had opened up; manufacturing was struggling; the Detroit automakers were clearly in trouble. But what were we to do about it? President Jimmy Carter opted for the usual thing, appointing a blue-ribbon advisory committee to study America’s innovation system and find out what ailed it. It in turn produced a massive report that made only minuscule recommendations. Others, however, spoke out with what seemed like brilliant clarity. This time around they did not blame conformity or crass, chrome-plated cars. It was Big Government, they said, that was crushing America’s creativity. Their solutions were simple and direct, and they got their way. In 1978, Congress slashed capital gains taxes on the grounds that doing so would reinvigorate the spirit of innovation. The Steiger Amendment, the measure was called: written by a Republican, passed by a Democratic Congress, and signed by a Democratic president, it was the first shot in the long and noisy tax-cut revolution that goes on to this day. A curious detail about Ronald Reagan, the man who defeated Carter in 1980 and put the rollback of government into high gear: he was very fond of the word “creative.” The Creative Society was the title he gave to a collection of his speeches, and unleashing creativity was his polestar as he launched his market-oriented revolution. In 1988, he looked back with satisfaction on his achievements and spoke of a “new economy,” a sort of accelerated version of postindustrialism, in which capital was free to zip around the world electronically and “labor” had come to mean “the creativity of the writer of computer software.” This new economy, Reagan said, was outside the control of any kind of establishment: “It’s driven from the ground up by our new heroes, the entrepreneurs, the explorers of the modern era, who conceive, create, and produce, and in doing so discover the future one piece at a time.” In this new understanding, creativity was identified not so much with artists or countercultural youth but with the act of entrepreneurship, the starting-up of a business. As the supply-side philosopher George Gilder put it in 1984, “The key to growth is quite simple: creative men with money. The cause of stagnation is similarly clear: depriving creative individuals of financial power.” Creative people would deliver prosperity, so long as we deferred to them and made sure their taxes were low. Gilder went on: “An economy is governed by the will and imagination, creativity and persistence of its entrepreneurs. All that matters is that they be encouraged . . . to do their work well.” The disassembly of the old liberal state has been a decades-long project, and at every step in the demolition, these ideas were what got the job done. Creativity and innovation were, persistently and comprehensively, the cover story for the neoliberal revolution. We privatized university research — and universities themselves, in effect — on the grounds that the profit motive would reinvigorate the creativity of the highly educated. We deregulated banks because we thought “financial innovation” would make us all rich. We wrote trade agreements that undermined the livelihoods of the blue-collar class because we knew it did not innovate. We offshored manufacturing because, in a postindustrial “new economy,” only creative work was worthy of protection and respect. A zenith of some kind was reached during the presidency of Barack Obama, who understood innovation as the paramount object of enlightened governance. In a famous speech in 2011 he acknowledged the “painful disruptions” that were tearing the middle class apart, but even so, he insisted that in an “innovation economy” the only real answer was more and better education. Obama mentioned “innovation” or “innovators” in all seven of his State of the Union speeches, he proposed an “Innovation Agenda,” he published a series of innovation manifestos, and the executive branch resonated enthusiastically to the new imperative. The State Department, for example, launched the Transatlantic Innovation Action Partnership, the US-India Innovation Exchange, the NEXUS Innovation Initiative, the Global Innovation through Science and Technology program, and the American Innovation Roadshow. The Smithsonian dubbed 2015 the “Year of Innovation.” So committed was the Defense Department to the golden idea that, in one thirty-eight-minute speech in 2016, Secretary Ashton Carter managed to use some version of the word “innovation” sixty-seven times, calling for greater creativity in every aspect of warmaking and carefully name-checking the era’s great tech CEOs. All these momentous efforts, undertaken over the decades to revive innovation and creativity . . . and yet the twin gods have never really returned. Writing and music and liberal-arts academia are career dead ends today, as everyone knows. Culturally speaking, the country is obviously stagnant, with its classic rock and its superhero movies. Politically, we are in an endless loop of the old identity politics versus backlash wars of the 1970s. We still drive cars and live in suburbs and travel on jet planes and blast our enemies with B-52s. And despite our tax cutting and our deregulating and even despite our very real advances in computers and telecommunications, productivity growth today lags well behind the pace of the ’50s and ’60s. Even in the unhappy year 1978, the economy grew at a rate of 5.5 percent, much greater than what we ordinarily achieve nowadays. But we modern Americans have succeeded in discovering levels of inequality unknown to our ancestors. Today what economists call the “ labor share ” of national income is at all-time lows, as blue-collar workers are tossed overboard from the middle class. What we might call the “creative share,” meanwhile, is at all-time highs. In 1978, there were only two known billionaires in the United States. Today there are close to a thousand, cornering this market or that one, jacking up the price of medicine, injecting millions into political campaigns, collecting art, dispensing wisdom to the eager crowds at SXSW, building their end-times fortresses, chirping about how AI might end humanity, achieving remarkable levels of spiritual enlightenment, and absorbing the praise of the world for their innovativeness, their amazing powers of creativity. Sometimes it feels as though the old middle-class society was undone by its dreams. “Equality is the antithesis of creativity,” an education magazine instructed Americans back in 1960. But we never understood the contradiction or considered the oligarchic downside. We loved equality and yet valued creativity over almost everything else: this is what we wanted for every child, the vague but all-American form of brilliance that would give us artistic achievement and spiritual satisfaction at the same time. It was a short walk from there to the cultlike adulation we routinely express for Steve Jobs , innovator and prophet, billionaire son of the old middle class. Maybe the truth is that those creative billionaires are the only ones who really matter. “The creative person in a sense does something for all of us simply by being,” the psychologist Frank Barron declared back in the heady year 1969, “and perhaps we help ourselves when we help such persons in the process of their own creative unfolding.” Maybe their creativity trickles down to the rest of us the same way material prosperity is transmitted. Maybe building an elite that breaks things and smokes weed and cavorts around onstage with a deregulatory chainsaw is the best any nation can ask for. We gape and cheer and marvel at their enlightenment, for we know they elevate the rest of us simply by being. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
