articles.title: The Strange Power of You Can See Everything
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s fascinating documentary You Can See Everything is now the object of obsession for moviegoers everywhere. It’s a pretty exciting moment, groups of friends racing off to the theater, talking avidly in the parking lot afterward, going home to think about it some more, seeking out more friends with whom to hash it out all over again. If you haven’t seen it and you’re not “in on it” yet, fix that immediately. This doesn’t happen often in our moviegoing world. The initial source of obsession is the basic wow factor of the film, which is codirectors Fielder and Oppenheim’s assured ability to make you toggle back and forth for hours between two broad assessments of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced health tech CEO of Theranos, currently doing time for fraud in a minimum-security Texas prison. In constantly proclaiming her innocence, is Holmes just a cynical, manipulative liar? Or is it actually possible that she is somehow, in some complicated way, an innocent — someone who “thinks differently,” is perhaps neurodivergent, and may be held in a kind of emotional bondage by the men in her life like her current partner Billy Evans and her former boyfriend, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, the ex-chief operating officer of Theranos, who are the real baddies in the scenario? Nobody’s questioning whether fraud was committed, at least not for long — interrogator Fielder starts off making it clear that he doesn’t believe her. Holmes’s Theranos invention was marketed on the claim that it could test a single drop of blood for a huge number of diseases and conditions with maximum efficiency, an incredible claim that was never borne out in practical tests. Yet Theranos took in vast funding dollars from a consortium of old rich guys who were particularly susceptible to Holmes’s baby-faced blonde appeal. But the longer Fielder interviews her, the more he sees her as an enigma, if only because she’s claiming such an inhuman level of transparency in offering up “my truth.” The film’s title is drawn from an offer she makes to him, via text, to come and document the lives of her and her family in the month before she goes to prison: “You can see everything.” At a certain point in the process, Fielder even moves in with them, doubling down on Holmes’s commitment to revealing all to him. Fielder himself, in interviews promoting the film, asks repeatedly the question he claims still preoccupies him: “Why would you want to spend your last month of freedom [before a decade in prison] with this guy?” Why Nathan Fielder of All People? In other words, why would a woman invite awkward, deadpan, cringe-comedy king Nathan Fielder and his film crew to infest her home and family life? At such a terrible time, he’s hardly a comforting presence. And even the most cursory googling will reveal the sort of media figure Fielder is and the agonizing lengths he goes to in probing the most uncomfortable and often bleakly funny areas of human interaction. If Holmes wants a documentary showing her in a warm and cuddly way that might improve her public image, perhaps even a path to a post-prison comeback, there are countless hacks in the world of documentaries who’d be happy to oblige. But consider the first filmmaker Holmes and Davis approached: Errol Morris of The Thin Blue Line (1988), Mr. Death: The Rise and Fall of Fred A. Leuchter, Jr . (1999), and The Fog of War (2003). Morris is, or once was, the other most uncomfortably probing media-maker, the one who came up with the “three-minute rule,” the length of time the director and his camera stare at the person being interviewed after asking a question. Morris claimed he’d determined that no one can withstand three full minutes of silent staring — it cracks the strongest — the most wary, reticent, secretive interviewee will start spilling their guts. You see the pattern here. Though Holmes claims she had no clear idea who Nathan Fielder was, it seems clear that somebody did. It may be whole point of this documentary was to create the clash of the titans, to pit Holmes’s wide-eyed unbroken gaze to a documentary filmmaker who thinks he can out-stare her, break her down, get her to confess to lying, fraud, cynical manipulation. And if he can’t do it, well — that could stand as a kind of “reasonable doubt” in the public mind. According to John Carreyrou, the journalist who broke the Theranos scandal, Holmes had previously hired Morris in 2016 to make “sleek Theranos commercials at the height of her pre-scandal fame.” Post-scandal, she approached Morris about making the documentary. Morris was interested, and inquired if Carreyrou would be willing to participate, saying, “I see it as a ‘he said, she said,’” scenario. Carreyrou flatly rejected this characterization, saying, “That’s not how I see it. There are basic facts, and those facts show Elizabeth Holmes committed fraud.” Again, according to Carreyrou, Morris later indicated that, though he didn’t dispute Holmes’s guilt, he “wanted to explore the theme of self-deception.” Obviously, we’ll never know what Morris’s version would’ve looked like beyond the certainty of the epic stare down. But Fielder and Oppenheim’s film, which premiered a scant six weeks ago at the Telluride Film Festival, caused an immediate sensation. It was quickly slotted into theaters and marketed on its extraordinary preview, showing Nathan Fielder — whose flat probing stare is well known to those who’ve seen his remarkable cringe-comedy television series Nathan for You and The Rehearsal — facing off in a close-up stare down with Elizabeth Holmes, whose own big blue-eyed stare, absolutely unblinking, seemed to make it a mysterious attempt at offering up proof of her own purity and honesty. Look at how transparent those eyes are, like a newborn baby’s! Elizabeth Holmes’s Viral Stare This image of Holmes’s face drawn from the film went viral. And in You Can See Everything , it becomes the main site of interrogation because, for one thing, her ability to stare at such length is physically bizarre. If you try it yourself, you quickly find how painful it is not to blink for, say, a full minute. Actors adopt the unblinking stare as an extreme performance device that is guaranteed to weird out audiences — Anthony Hopkins used it to play Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs . The comedian Josh Jackson has a whole stand-up routine built around that mad, impossible, unbearable stare of Elizabeth Holmes. Holmes poses a challenge to film’s supposed capacity to reveal what can’t be seen with the naked eye. Early film theorists, seeking to define the compelling new medium, used to expound extensively on the power of the filmed close-up of the human face to show us what no one could see in real life. Projected far beyond life-size, the close-up seems to show us every slight movement of facial muscles, every passing shift in expression. The old province of painting, “capturing the soul of the sitter” posing before the all-seeing eye of the artist, seemed to have given way to this far more revealing mechanical media form. You Can See Everything goes far beyond the intensive, mesmerizing interactions of Fielder and Holmes, continuing past the point when Holmes goes to prison and becomes almost entirely inaccessible. Her partner and the father of her children, Billy Evans, becomes the subject of filmed interrogation, in addition to one more startling figure I can’t name because it’s a spoiler. But safe to say, each of these new subjects of the documentary, who are also performers before the camera with agendas of their own, shift the ground of interrogation in such dramatic ways, audiences are exclaiming aloud, often in unison, as they’re swayed this way and that in shockingly emotional twists and turns. Fielder and Oppenheim are not in the least shy about deploying several devices from the world of scripted filmmaking, including genre conventions drawn from gothic melodrama, suspense films, and the paranoid conspiracy thriller. For example, the tense, thrumming score by Ari Balouzian, who worked with Oppenheim on Primetime , also out this month, deliberately evokes Vertigo , a film about a man whose fantasy obsession with a woman finally drives him insane. Late in the film, “the ticking clock,” one of the tritest conventions of suspense films, becomes a driving force in keying up the audience to a fever pitch of angst. You can recognize all these conventions as they appear and still be swept away by the power of You Can See Everything . I was so dazzled by the film that I could think of only one director, Alfred Hitchcock, who was better at making audiences fully aware of his films’ artifice while still manipulating their emotions as effectively as if they were the most naive of viewers. Fielder and Oppenheim’s Agenda Which gives rise to the question — as you round into hour three of You Can See Everything , even more enthralled than you were in hour one — what are Fielder and Oppenheim trying to accomplish here? It certainly goes far beyond the question of whether Elizabeth Holmes is a lying grifter or not, though many critics and commentators seem stuck on that basic question. As she seems to draw even Fielder into a more and more emotionally addled relationship — and as you begin to wonder how much Fielder is at least partially performing that addled state for the purpose of further addling you, the viewer — you start the Vertigo -like spiraling into undecidability that is both deeply uncomfortable and yet hypnotically irresistible. What is this power of persuasion that some people possess, so potent it seems to warp time and space around them? It’s a question that troubled ancient Greek and Roman rhetoricians as they grappled with the dangers of sophistry. How much are Fielder and Oppenheim seeking to both study and demonstrate it through cinematic manipulation? How much are you, the viewer, implicated in your own constant shadings of the truth and outright lies and impromptu performances in order to grease the wheels of your own difficult passage through life, surrounded by other fibbers, scammers, and playactors? If Elizabeth Holmes’s face comes to horrify you after you’ve gazed at its infantile blankness long enough, and if Nathan Fielder’s deadpan also begins to agitate you, what is your own face doing as you present it to others out in the world? For Halloween horror viewing, look no further than You Can See Everything , a film that only grows eerier in the days after you’ve seen it, drawing viewers back to the theater to determine whether they really saw what they thought they saw. It’s truly one of a kind. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: America in Retreat
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. As always, the Trump administration is setting ever stranger records for public “entertainment” (and yes, I certainly do have to put that word in quotation marks). Only recently, Secretary of–you choose–War/Defense (I certainly know which I’d choose) Pete Hegseth made it clear that Nidal Hassan, a former U.S. Army psychiatrist and American-born Muslim, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Ft. Hood, Texas, in 2009 ( claiming to be waging jihad “for what he called the illegal and immoral wars in Afghanistan and Iraq”), would be executed by a military firing squad on December 3rd and that the killing would–a first–be “live-streamed” for–obviously!–public entertainment. (The last time a member of the U.S. military was even executed by firing squad was for desertion in France on January 31, 1945, only months before World War II ended in Europe.) And just to put such a plan in perspective, these days, on this planet of ours, the only other two countries that regularly carry out public executions of capital sentences are Afghanistan and Iran. Even Saudi Arabia has stopped doing so (which should tell you something about the company the United States is now keeping). In this country, nothing quite like this has happened since the public hanging of Rainey Bethea , a Black confessed rapist and killer, in Owensburg, Kentucky, in 1936, witnessed by an estimated 20,000 onlookers. Ever since then, execution as a public spectacle has been forbidden. But evidently, in the age of Donald Trump, nothing, however grim, is truly forbidden anymore, though, of course, the president did finally have to break down and, while not stopping the firing-squad execution, cancel its public screening . Buy the Book In fact, in some strange sense, that public firing-squad execution, had it actually happened (and there certainly was opposition to it , even among congressional Republicans, though not, of course, from the president of the United States), would have been all too symbolic of the age of Trump and of a country that is distinctly going down, down, down on a planet that is, in fact, doing the same . This may simply no longer be a Trumpian planet in any sense of the term. Give him full credit, of course. He’s been nothing short of amazing (or rather amazingly bizarre) during one and a half presidencies (so far), especially since, once upon a time, the very idea of him as president of the United States would have been the most ridiculous joke imaginable–or do I mean unimaginable? He should, in fact, be all too literally considered the living definition of imperial decline. And yes, it’s true that Executioner-in-Chief Donald Trump is also now in retreat on almost every front imaginable, from global politics to the American version of the same. Don’t doubt for a second, for instance, that his party is likely to get clobbered in the upcoming November congressional elections, even though American billionaires are spending a fortune to help Republican candidates. After all, it looks like all too many of his potential voters might simply stay home, a phenomenon already labeled “the red undertow.” Related: Trump's America: Failing, Flailing, and Falling Decline at Sea? Globally, once upon a time, who would have even believed this version of the United States? Admittedly, there was that disastrous Vietnam War in the previous century, but still, this country remained a power beyond compare as its competitor, the Soviet Union, collapsed. These days, however, in the age (or do I mean the aging?) of Donald Trump, it’s down, down, down, and down again. In fact, retreat now seems to be distinctly the name of the game. As a recent New York Times headline bluntly summed it up : “Trump’s Retreat: From the Gulf to Britain, American Forces Pull Back.” That, of course, was in relation to the war he launched against Iran which, if you happen to remember, was going to be victoriously ended within weeks. Seven months later, he’s talking about pursuing it yet again in a big-time fashion after the November congressional elections. Here’s how he explains it : “I stated, numerous times, that it would take 4-6 weeks to get rid of THE IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, and I did it in one night!... the rest of the time is just to make sure it stays that way.” It all makes sense now, right? And give him credit: seven months later, there indeed is no Iranian nuclear threat (not that there ever was). In that sense he couldn’t have been more successful or, as he put it , “I am ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. We had no choice because we can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.” Oh, now I understand, of course. (Who wouldn’t?) And under the circumstances, what a success his war has been! Success and yet... once upon a time, “our” president certainly never would have guessed that, so many months after he launched his war, for fear of an Iranian attack, his administration would actually have pulled back a set of B-1 bombers from... no, not Saudi Arabia or Jordan (not faintly!), but Great Britain. Yes, those bombers were withdrawn from a base in England to bases in the United States, which couldn’t have been more victorious of him, could it? It fits perfectly with that TV show he (and I) once watched as kids about the U.S. Navy in World War II, Victory at Sea . Related: We're Up Shit's Creek Without a Paddle—and Trump Is Steering And that tells you all too much about this increasingly strange planet (and president) of ours and just how Donald Trump and crew are taking down possibly the greatest imperial power ever in a big-time fashion. It should also give you a sense of just how disastrous Trump’s war on Iran, which he claimed last spring would end “I think within maybe two weeks, maybe a couple of days longer, to do the job,”–and (it goes without saying) in victory, of course–has proven to be. These days, in fact, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are both suggesting that the war might last all the way through his second presidency. Yes, Donald Trump is finally being pummeled on this planet of– well, is it ours or his?–and he’s undoubtedly soon going to be pummeled again, right here in the United States, a country with staggering numbers of nuclear weapons, in the upcoming November congressional races, where it will be beyond surprising if he and his party don’t go down, down, down. Yes, whether he even knows it or not, he is now in retreat in a big-time fashion, including on that public execution. That includes, of course, his retreat from his recent comments about Los Angeles and San Diego being potentially lost to (assumedly) an Iranian nuclear weapon (that, of course, doesn’t exist) and that, were such a thing to happen, really wouldn’t matter to him. Yes, who among us would truly care if two West Coast, pro-Democratic cities were lost to Iranian nukes? Not “our” president, that’s for sure! And let me just suggest that, after this November 3rd, President Trump is likely to find himself in retreat big time in American politics, too. Here’s the truth of the matter: when the president of the United States (and some of his top officials like Pete Hegseth) are in retreat mode, whether we know it or not, we’re in a different world. Related: Trump, Endless Wars, and the Decline of American Empire Honestly, the coming of Donald Trump as president of (not so long ago) the most powerful and dominant country on the planet gives imperial decline new meaning. Honestly (yet again!), once upon a time, it would have been hard to imagine any great imperial power, no less the United States of America, having someone like Donald Trump as president even in its era of decline. His very existence (twice!) as president of the United States suggests that decline has new meaning on a planet that itself may be going down in a big-time fashion. Perhaps a future TV series about the U.S. military in his presidency will be called “Decline at Sea.” Retreat, ho! Tom's Substack

articles.title: Columbus DSA stands in Solidarity with Ilhan Omar
articles.author: Columbus DSA
articles.content: The Columbus chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) extends our full support to Representative Ilhan Omar in the face of racist and xenophobic campaigns against her by the Trump Administration and the fascist right wing. The targeting of Rep. Omar escalated on Monday, October 12, with the unprecedented raid of her Washington, DC home by the Trump Administration’s Department of Justice (DOJ). The DOJ has claimed that it is investigating possible “immigration fraud” committed by Rep. Omar, a baseless conspiracy theory for which no evidence has ever been produced, even after years of targeting by the far right. But the real aim of the assault is clear: to vilify and silence Rep. Omar in the weeks before the midterm elections, create a pretext for efforts to deport her, and stoke further xenophobia and Islamophobia against Somali communities across the country. The Trump Administration’s campaign of terror against Rep. Omar and our Somali neighbors, from ICE’s “Operation Metro Surge” in Minneapolis to its “Operation Buckeye” here in Columbus, is both a continuation and a serious escalation of the bipartisan targeting of all immigrants and refugees – with and without documentation. While this policy of state xenophobia has especially characterized the last two decades, from President Obama’s role as the “Deporter-in-Chief” to President Trump’s openly fascist policies of mass deportation and attacks on birthright citizenship, it is a long-standing policy of the American ruling class. From the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 to the Laken Riley Act of 2025, the scapegoating of immigrants and refugees has continually served to turn working people against each other, obscure our shared interests in organizing together, and deflect our class anger from where it belongs: the capitalist class that exploits us all. As socialists, we categorically reject these transparent attempts to divide us from our neighbors. Representative Ilhan Omar continues to be one of the most principled fighters against imperialism and fascism in American politics, and her refusal to be silenced in the face of mounting attacks is an inspiration to all of us. Columbus DSA expresses our full and unequivocal solidarity with Rep. Omar, and we encourage everyone to share her asks for support in this fight.

articles.title: We Can Beat the Right With a Left-Wing Affordability Agenda
articles.author: Niko Block
articles.content: In the past decade, much ink has been spilled over the question of whether we are witnessing a resurgence of fascism. Those debates have calmed since last November, when Donald Trump casually identified himself as a fascist amid a disorientingly effusive meeting with New York City’s Mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani. Part of the problem with the debate is that fascism can be difficult to define and identify — a point economist Isabella Weber makes at the outset of her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics . Unlike other major political ideologies, fascism has few defining texts, social theories, or economic platforms. However, she adds, there are “unifying themes — and an obsession with restoring the dominance of the chosen group by authoritarian and violent means is key.” To my mind, fascist ideology is captured well enough by its original symbol, the fasces: a hatchet made of tightly bound rods and an axe head, representing the fierce unity of the nation on the one hand and its outward-facing aggression on the other. As Matt Christman once described it, “The cultural expression of fascism is a Janus face of performative sentimentality and performative cruelty.” To take the point a little further, fascism’s programmatic vagueness means that we may in fact be on better footing if we regard it as a cultural phenomenon with political aspirations. That is more or less the approach offered by Weber and by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor in their equally insightful new book, End Times Fascism . Both books make a persuasive case that the contemporary swell of revanchism has resulted from rising levels of economic stress and valid anxieties across vast swathes of Global North society. When a sense of scarcity takes hold, the Right can make a compelling argument for the abandonment of solidaristic values in favor of bunkerism. That we are confronting this crisis in a moment of unprecedented levels of automation and global integration points to a profound failure of the neoliberal doctrines that have shaped the global system. Weber’s work offers one of the most systematic critiques of those doctrines, as well as a plausible set of alternative policies. At the heart of her argument is a basic refutation of the neoliberal position that there is no viable middle ground between a totalitarian command economy and the free market. Indeed, as she notes repeatedly, neoliberals have consistently shown a preference for free-market authoritarianism over social democracy. Today, she argues, we must recognize that the latter is more viable than mainstream thought has led us to believe. The intellectual leaders of neoliberalism — notably Friedrich Hayek and Milton Friedman — are best known for their attacks on the modern welfare state. But an equally central neoliberal dogma is that price controls are necessarily doomed to fail in private markets, so that governments must choose between comprehensive price-setting or complete laissez-faire. The standard price mechanism suggests that if prices are set too low, there will be a shortage of goods; too high, and there will be a surfeit of unsold product. One of the essential premises of modern economic thought is that the ideal market-clearing price can only be determined in fully private markets. This second argument has conquered Northern minds almost completely for the past half-century, making it one of the most sacred cows in modern economic thought. Weber reveals that this faith is unwarranted. Simply put, it does not follow from the standard price mechanism that commodity markets should be fully private or unregulated. The problem is not merely that private markets fall prey to monopolistic power; it is that they are prone to crises that exacerbate poverty and inequality. Supply shocks can emerge from environmental disasters, wars, and pandemics — and when this occurs, prices will spike in the affected industries, with potentially dangerous political effects. As Weber puts it, “Commodity markets are inherently volatile, and the human cost of leaving them entirely to private participants falls hardest on those least able to absorb it, while carrying the potential to destabilize whole economies and societies.” This argument, drawing from neglected histories of successful price control policies, amounts to a significant departure from the prevailing wisdom. The option of price controls is especially vital because, she argues, mainstream economists have gravely mischaracterized the drivers of inflation: far from an excess of demand, the main problem is a form of “sellers’ inflation,” which occurs when price shocks facilitate corporate price gouging at the expense of the general public. Her work thus points in a clear direction for anyone seeking practical strategies for economic stabilization in an era of overlapping crises. For those seeking a theoretical doctrine, the conclusions are less clear, but a search for doctrine would miss the point. Weber begins with real-world observation, rather than abstract behavioral models. Likewise, the mixed-market approach she proposes would require continuous fine-tuning and is therefore intrinsically resistant to oversimplification. In reality, there is no one-size-fits-all policy prescription across all industries in all countries. Rather, policy must be designed through a process of careful experimentation, observation, and revision. That Weber leaves some questions open, rather than giving pat answers from outmoded theories, is precisely what makes her work so exciting. Indeed, a central challenge for contemporary socialists is to consider how her vital insights on industrial policy can fit into a broader left-wing agenda. The First Anti-Fascist Economists For Weber, many of the Left’s twentieth-century darlings should be understood as the founders of anti-fascist economics: from the world of theory, Karl Polanyi, John Maynard Keynes, Michał Kalecki; from the world of policy, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and his pricing czar, John Kenneth Galbraith. As she reflects on the 1930s and ’40s, the contemporary relevance of their perspective becomes clear. The Great Depression was instigated by a frenzy of speculation that ended in financial calamity; from there it spread to the international system as a result of misguided adherence to the gold standard. In Germany, the centrist chancellor, Heinrich Brüning, adopted a textbook policy of austerity, exacerbating the crises of unaffordability and unemployment while “business elites and orthodox economists cheered him on,” writes Weber. Several important lessons emerge from this episode. For Polanyi, observing the crisis unfold from nearby Vienna, “The victory of fascism was made practically unavoidable by the liberals’ obstruction of any reform involving planning, regulation, or control.” Second, countercyclical expansionary policies may boost employment as well as profits, but many capitalists nonetheless oppose such interventions because these threaten their political power. On this point, Weber draws from Kalecki’s incisive argument that business elites typically oppose government programs that would generate full employment and thus strengthen workers’ bargaining power. The business community therefore seeks to retain its control over “the state of confidence” in the economy and accepts the cyclical volatility this entails. Often their cause is championed in the public sphere by “prominent so-called ‘economic experts’ closely connected with banking and industry.” In this light, authoritarianism can be especially appealing to elites, as the state actively stokes industry — especially in weapons production — yet at the same time keeps wages down by force. Third, the Left can also contribute to crisis when it puts doctrine ahead of observation. On this point, Weber observes that the German Social Democrats sustained an ideological commitment to the gold standard because their dominant in-house economist, Rudolf Hilferding, believed it vindicated the Marxian labor theory of value. Fourth, economists’ promises that short-term suffering is necessary for long-run stabilization should be dismissed as millenarian superstition. As Keynes put it, “In the long run we are all dead.” Indeed, he added, “Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that when the storm is long past the ocean is flat again.” Short-term crises — such as Germany’s 1923 hyperinflation or its 1931 fiscal and banking crisis — can have irreversible consequences when we account for human behavior in the real world. Even brief periods of deprivation can give rise to a political logic of sadistic authoritarianism that soon takes on a life of its own. Rethinking Inflation The present moment is more of a rhyme with, rather than a repetition of, the 1930s. But it is hard to ignore the parallel behaviors of a political establishment that lacks courage, ignores evidence, and disingenuously takes advice from business elites. In some ways, the waves of crises have been slower moving, but there are more of them, and they will persist for a long while. The 2008 financial crisis spread from Wall Street throughout the global economy, and this time was approached with some degree of countercyclical stabilization — but that was followed by austerity. Consequently, inequality surged across many Northern economies, affordability declined in many areas, and a new wave of political bigotry arose to critique the Brüning-esque centrists who claimed there was no other option. The pandemic and subsequent war in Ukraine brought a whole new round of crisis: a wave of inflation that hit several economies at once. In response, economists working from textbook theories of inflation called for a new round of austerity. Those theories, the Phillips curve and the “non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment” (or NAIRU), insist that when employment rates are too high, spendthrift workers will push prices up to a self-defeating extent. Hence the appropriate solution, they claim, is to raise unemployment through fiscal austerity and monetary tightening (i.e., high interest rates). As Weber notes, the evidence for these ideas is weak . Despite multiple attempts, economists have never actually identified the NAIRU; it is something “like a unicorn, a recurring reference in the literature but never observed in real life.” The underlying problem, she wrote in a series of papers and op-eds during the inflationary episode, was not excess demand but sellers’ inflation. Her central argument is that when supply shocks occur in “systemically significant” sectors like oil, they can cause uneven ripple effects across the rest of the market. Because oil is an input in countless other goods, many producers passed on the price shock by raising their sale prices — an echo of the 1970s inflation wave that followed from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) oil embargo. In these moments when businesses concurrently boost prices, a secondary logic can take hold. In concentrated markets, the price signal allows sellers to effectively collude by hiking prices in tandem, “without anything so direct as a ‘conversation.’” This allows them to overcompensate for their losses and secure windfall profits at the expense of the broader public. (That this is a real and deliberate phenomenon is clear; one of Weber’s many papers surveys transcripts from 138,962 corporate earnings calls and finds that top managers tend to speak positively about inflation because it enables profit-enhancing price hikes.) The distributional effects of sellers’ inflation have been especially pernicious, because it hit essential goods harder than luxury goods. This occurred partly because the market is highly concentrated in certain essential sectors — especially food but also household staples like diapers — and partly because of the inelastic nature of essentials; you can’t do without them. In this context, monetary tightening does more harm than good, by elevating unemployment as well as debt servicing costs. It also disrespects precarious individuals in ways that stoke a politics of resentment. Consider, writes Weber, what it must be like to be laid off in this context and then see someone like Larry Summers on TV “saying that people like you should lose their jobs so that prices would come back down. The natural response is rage.” The far right, she adds, has cannily exploited that rage: “They have tapped into it, fueled it, and abused it with false promises.” For many reasons, then, sellers’ inflation calls for a completely different set of policy responses. The first is a steep tax on windfall profits to disincentivize collusive price gouging. (Something like this, Weber notes, was vaguely floated by Kamala Harris early in her campaign and then meekly buried .) Second, because fossil fuels are the most systemically significant commodities, the transition to renewable energy is easily among the most important stabilization strategies. Here she cites Brett Christophers’s important point that a green transition cannot be expected to occur just because the price of renewable energy has declined below that of fossil fuels. Renewables are fundamentally different in that they are “a stock of capital goods” and “not a flow of inputs.” They do not yield short-term profits, and indeed they are financially riskier, especially in moments of monetary tightening. Private capital therefore cannot be expected to build the renewable infrastructure we need. In this context, even carbon pricing policies (like cap-and-trade or carbon taxes) are bound to fail. Absent renewable infrastructure, these costs are simply passed on to frustrated consumers. Third, Weber calls for active government policies that would “steer, manage or provision essentials.” On the provisioning side, she defends a revitalization of public education, transportation, and health care under a framework of “universal basic services.” However, it is on the steering and management side that Weber makes her central intervention. Her flagship policy proposal is the use of buffer stocks to smooth out supply shocks when they occur. Contrary to the neoliberal story, Weber’s work reveals that the state can in fact regulate prices by creating substantial reserves of nonperishable goods — especially food and fossil fuels — by buying en masse when they are cheap and selling when prices rise. While the production of these goods can fluctuate, demand for them remains relatively stable and predictable because of their essential nature. Price controls can therefore be entirely viable if they are implemented through supply management, rather than mere fiat. In the present book, an exemplary case study is the FDR-Galbraith administration during World War II, which sustained effective price controls despite limited institutional experience with them. Weber also highlights China’s much deeper history of price management, which was the central focus of her dissertation and first book , How China Escaped Shock Therapy . She shows that Chinese governments have been engaged in price controls for centuries, and a major factor in the Communist Party’s victory in the 1940s was its success in taming inflation through supply management in the areas that it captured. In the post–Mao Zedong era, China maintained economic sovereignty in ways that many other countries did not and invited policy proposals from a community of economists who were practically minded, empirically informed, and arguably more intellectually diverse than their counterparts in the West. The resulting compromises delivered a policy approach of “crossing the river by feeling for stones.” For instance, the state experimented with price liberalization in areas where the party wanted fast growth and reined it in when inflation started to surge — a policy machinery that would respond proactively to volatility. Returning to the present decade, Weber discusses the pandemic response in Mexico, which “offers perhaps the most impressive recent example of a creative and ambitious inflation policy.” Under Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO), the government constrained prices on an essential basket of goods (including corn, beans, and rice) with partnering grocers, who in turn were rewarded with reduced transport fees and relaxed regulatory requirements. At the same time, AMLO’s government stoked domestic production through a program that allowed small farmers to sell to the government reserves at a guaranteed minimum price. The success of these policies carries an important lesson: It is better to be prepared, because buffer stocks cannot be magically conjured when a crisis strikes; yet at the same time, active management of price and supply can be achieved on relatively short notice. In either case, the implementation of these progressive policies can offer major gains for politicians who are courageous enough to put government capacity to work in defiance of corporate elites. Price Controls and the Broader Vision Over many decades, mainstream economists have constructed an edifice in which progressive ideas can hardly be uttered. Yet the arguments behind this stifling decorum are weak, as many hard-nosed progressives have demonstrated. Keynes and his followers have disproven the assumption that the savings of the rich are a precondition for growth-inducing investment. Similarly, contemporary economists like Joseph Stiglitz have shown that redistribution does not stymie growth, as neoliberals claim. Weber’s demonstration that price controls are not only viable but wise should be regarded as yet another embarrassment for the masters of the house. These and other failures of mainstream economics should signal to those of us who believe in economic justice that it is time to exit the castle, to a place where we can speak more freely. But where exactly would we go? That question is not fully answered by Weber, but she gives a sense of direction; readers of Anti-Fascist Economics who seek either an overarching theoretical critique of capitalism or a detailed policy agenda will not find everything they’re looking for. Weber is explicit that what she offers “are not blueprints but starting points.” There is no detailed master plan for a revitalization of the welfare state, or concrete engagement with broader issues of taxes and transfers. Thorough analyses and ambitious reforms on this topic have, in any case, already been advanced by Thomas Piketty and his colleagues , and these proposals — especially the effective income ceiling — are complementary to Weber’s vision. Still, Anti-Fascist Economics could have benefited from broader engagement with the core topic of inflation. It gives a strong analysis of commodity inflation, but it misses two other types of inflation: hyperinflation and housing inflation. Hyperinflation is relevant to Weber’s argument mostly because mainstream economists like to cite a few catastrophic episodes when the rate of inflation reached millions of percent — Germany in 1923, Hungary in 1946, or Zimbabwe in 2008 — as evidence of the necessity of monetary discipline. In fact, hyperinflation is qualitatively different from the more frequent dynamic of sellers’ inflation and usually occurs when an industrially fragile, import-dependent country runs out of foreign currency and cannot meet its foreign-denominated obligations. Governments facing such a crisis have occasionally chosen to break the rules of central banking by issuing new monetary assets without any expectation of repayment — and this is where true money printing can occur. When inflation sets in, residents are prone to sell their domestic currency in favor of a more stable foreign currency. This in turn devalues the domestic currency on foreign markets, so that imports become more expensive. At this point, the economy can easily slide into an “inflation-depreciation spiral” that is difficult to escape. Weber gestures to this distinct dynamic by noting that the German hyperinflation was “not triggered by sectoral cost shocks but by the inability of the government to pay back [its] enormous debts.” If she had extended the point a little further, she could have demonstrated that hyperinflation is a rare event, and one that does not threaten countries in the Global North that borrow in their own currency and can safely finance their imports. The issue, then, is that Weber misses an opportunity to discredit conservative arguments that use the threat of hyperinflation as a cudgel to defend fiscal and monetary austerity. The bigger lacuna is Weber’s light treatment of housing, which sits uncomfortably in her basket of essentials. It does not fit into her agenda of public provisioning quite as snugly as health care and education. At the same time, it is not the sort of good that lends itself to buffer stocks, like food and fuel. In the Global North, housing now follows an asset logic rather than a commodity logic, which means that the standard price mechanism at the heart of Weber’s analysis does not really apply. This is evident in studies showing that in the United States , Britain , and Canada , the stock of housing has in fact risen relative to population at the same time as it has become more unaffordable. Moreover, episodes of housing inflation become especially intense when interest rates are low — a scenario that complicates the critique of monetary tightening. We therefore require housing-specific policies that are qualitatively distinct from the buffer stock idea. To be clear, this does not represent a fatal flaw in Weber’s argument, and she does briefly address the problem by acknowledging the financialization of housing and calling for rent controls. My point, rather, is that we have yet to work out a holistic approach to inflation that covers both commodities and assets. Though Weber does not address every aspect of affordability, these gaps also have an inviting character, because it is clear that she wants Anti-Fascist Economics to contribute to a broader movement for economic justice. She and the many researchers with whom she collaborates have been uniquely effective in presenting their work to general audiences, promoting a broader understanding of macroeconomics while exposing neoliberal shibboleths. Certainly, her work helps to build the lines of communication between economics and the other social sciences — something that is sorely needed. Progressive political scientists have a habit of concluding their papers by blaming economic dynamics for the ills of the world, while progressive economists do the same but blame the government. Weber is one of very few left-wing economists who engages with the system as a whole and refuses to shrug off the work. articles.title: Peter Thomas Was a Marxist Intellectual With a Mission
articles.author: Max Tomba
articles.content: It is difficult to write in memory of Peter Thomas. Not for lack of memories, but because there are too many. So many discussions come to mind, shared projects, collective volumes to which we both contributed. One obvious one is In Marx’s Laboratory: Critical Interpretations of the Grundrisse (2013), which Peter coedited with Riccardo Bellofiore and Guido Starosta. But my thoughts turn even more insistently to The Government of Time: Theories of Plural Temporality in the Marxist Tradition (2017), coedited by Peter and Vittorio Morfino. The preparation of that volume was accompanied by countless discussions and meetings. I remember one in Milan, intellectually lively, friendly, and full of good humor. In those discussions, Peter had a remarkable ability to defuse tensions and soften the occasional sharp edges of disagreement without compromising the intellectual or political rigor of the exchange. He did so naturally, with a joke and a smile. But now other memories come flooding back. Peter, his family, his wife Sara, and their little girls. After I moved to California, it became more difficult for us to see each other and keep in touch. Yet only recently we had been in contact again, exchanging ideas and making plans for new projects. I had invited Peter to participate in a panel on my latest book, next month, at the Historical Materialism conference in London. He had gladly accepted and had already begun making plans for a dinner at his home. I still find it difficult to believe that I will not see him in London. I canceled the panel. It makes no sense to sit around discussing my book without Peter. A few months ago, I had also asked Peter to write a review essay for Political Theory , surveying the major publications and interpretive currents in Marx scholarship over the past twenty years. Peter had agreed, asking only for a little more time because he was overwhelmed with academic commitments. For five years, if I remember correctly, he had been serving as head of department in Brunel’s Department of Social and Political Sciences. I can’t help thinking: damn academic administration. Increasingly, it has become a machine that devours academics’ time, giving them in return stress, conflicts of every imaginable kind, and personality clashes that multiply in direct proportion to the loss of any intellectual meaning in academic work. Peter wanted to do research. He wanted to go on learning. He was a Gramscian who wanted to build a Marxist cultural hegemony. For him, Historical Materialism was precisely such a laboratory. That is why its growth mattered so much to him. It was not, and is not, simply a matter of numbers. It is about establishing and asserting a presence, developing a network of intellectual and political relationships. Peter once told me this himself. Peter believed in the political mission of the intellectual. At the heart of his intellectual project was a sustained effort to rethink the Gramscian concept of hegemony. Already in The Gramscian Moment (2009), Peter reconstructed hegemony as a central concept of Marxist political theory, inseparable from the formation of collective political capacities and the struggle for emancipation. His last book, Radical Politics: On the Causes of Contemporary Emancipation (2023), further developed this project, offering a powerful rethinking of politics beyond the alternatives of technocratic governance and populism. Hegemony, in this perspective, is not simply a form of domination secured through consent but a way of doing politics through which subordinated groups develop their capacities for collective action and self-government. It is a pedagogical practice, but not in the sense of intellectuals educating passive masses. After all, who educates the educators? Rather, political actors learn through collective experimentation, confrontation, organization, and the transformation of their own practices. This conception does not reject political leadership in the abstract. Rather, it understands leadership not as a power possessed by an individual or organization but as a relationship constituted and continually transformed through collective political activity. Leadership itself is transformed as that activity develops. “Protests without political direction are expressions of anger bordering on nihilism. Political leadership without the masses is empty vanguardist voluntarism. Intellectual work without concrete ties to politics and the anger of the masses is academic onanism.” This is how, many years ago, in a conversation with Peter in Padua, I summed up the agenda for the work that lay ahead. We never had the opportunity to return to that agenda, and I do not know how Peter might have reformulated it in light of the present. Looking back, however, I realize how much of this understanding of hegemony was already present in Peter’s own intellectual and political activity. His commitment to Historical Materialism, his efforts to bring together scholars from different countries and traditions, his generosity toward comrades: these were not simply expressions of an admirable personality. They were also part of a particular way of understanding intellectual work as political practice. I remember what struck me when I first met Peter. It was 2004 or 2005. Peter began telling me about his life in Naples, his research on Antonio Gramsci, and his connections with Neapolitan intellectuals and comrades. At the time, Peter, like so many of us, was a young scholar in a precarious position, moving around Europe. I was a few years older and had just secured a research position in Padua. Peter was traveling the length and breadth of Italy, seeking to build and consolidate a network of intellectual and political relationships. He was not simply going around meeting people. He was engaged in an intellectual and political project. Yet there was nothing instrumental about what he did. Quite the contrary: Peter did not ask for favors. He invited others to take part in a larger intellectual and political project. We discussed his approach to building such a project at length. I understood his point of view, but at the time I found it too ecumenical. Having been schooled in Amadeo Bordiga’s tradition, I believed we needed to be more selective. Better a few people, but the right ones. Peter helped me and other young Italian scholars break out of our provincial intellectual confines. In 2004, he encouraged me to participate in the Historical Materialism conference in London. My intellectual formation, shaped in Italy and Germany, had decidedly neglected the English language. To put it bluntly, my English was terrible. I told Peter as much. He smiled and replied, “Who gives a shit?” If this Australian cafone could speak Italian, he said, then surely you, Max, could speak English. I let myself be persuaded and went to London to present a paper on Walter Benjamin and violence. It was November 2005. With Peter’s help, I encouraged other Italian comrades to participate in Historical Materialism. For several years, a group of young researchers from Padua became regulars at the conference. Some of our publications were translated into English and published by Brill. Peter and Sara translated my book on Karl Marx and the layers of time, which they persuaded me to title Marx’s Temporalities . I was not the only one to publish with Brill. I remember Luca Basso, Vittorio Morfino, and Riccardo Bellofiore. Others deserve to be mentioned as well. What matters is that Peter helped us move beyond our provincial horizons, reach a wider audience, and make ourselves understood by anglophone readers. If that last task has not always been accomplished, the fault certainly does not lie with Peter. He helped us become part of a larger conversation, part of a larger network, and part of a hegemonic project. Did we succeed? Did we fail? These are the wrong questions, and there can be no right answers to the wrong questions. Hegemony, as Peter understood it, was not an achievement to be measured once and for all, but an ongoing practice of collective intellectual and political work. For those of us who had the good fortune to know Peter, to work with him, and to call him a comrade, keeping his memory alive means keeping that political project in motion. And, for those who can, it also means being there for his family. If I am now writing these lines from Santa Cruz, where I hold a position at the University of California, Peter played a part in making that possible. He encouraged me to venture into the anglophone world. He helped me break free from the provincialism of the Padua jargon, whose very essence he had grasped and loved to make fun of. That irony of his, and his generosity of spirit. How much I miss it, and how much I will go on missing it. articles.title: Equal Justice on the Road
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Every day, millions of people get behind the wheel trusting that others on the road will follow the rules. Most of the time, that trust holds. When it breaks, the results can change a life in seconds. A careless driver who runs a red light or checks a phone at the wrong moment can leave someone with injuries, medical bills, and months of lost income. In a large and busy city like Houston, where long commutes and crowded freeways are part of daily life, these moments happen far too often. The question that follows every crash is important: who will be held responsible, and will the injured person be treated fairly? Why Fair Treatment After a Crash Is Never Guaranteed After a serious collision, many people assume the system will take care of them and that the process will be quick and honest. An injured person often discovers that an attorney is needed, because the other side has trained staff whose job is to pay as little as possible. Skilled legal help gives ordinary people a fair chance to stand on equal footing with large companies. Many injured people choose to work with a trusted Houston car wreck attorney to understand their rights and pursue the full value of their claim. That kind of support often makes the difference between a quick, unfair offer and real accountability. How Insurance Companies Protect Their Own Interests Insurance companies are businesses, and like all businesses, they work to protect their profits. When a claim comes in, the company looks for ways to lower the amount it will pay. One common approach is the early offer. Shortly after an accident, an injured person may receive a call with a settlement offer that seems helpful at first. The problem is that many injuries do not show their full effects right away. Pain can grow worse over time, and treatment may last much longer than expected. Accepting an early offer usually means giving up the right to ask for more later. Another approach is shifting blame . An adjuster may suggest that the injured person was partly at fault, even when the facts point clearly to the other driver. If some of the blame sticks, the amount paid can drop. Recorded statements are often used for this purpose, which is why many people are careful about what they say in the days after a crash. The Real Cost of Negligence for Working Families A crash does not only damage cars. It can disrupt every part of a family's life. A parent who cannot work may struggle to pay rent or keep food on the table. A worker who relies on physical strength may find that an injury ends their ability to do their job. There are also costs that do not appear on any bill. Chronic pain, sleepless nights, anxiety behind the wheel, and missed time with loved ones all take a toll. These harms are real, and they deserve to be counted when responsibility is decided. For working families, the stakes are especially high. People with fewer savings have less room to wait for a fair outcome. This is exactly why low early offers can feel tempting, and why they can be so damaging in the long run. Steps Injured People Can Take to Protect Their Rights Ordinary people have more power than they may realize. Taking a few careful steps after a crash can make a big difference. The first step is getting medical care right away. Even if the injuries seem minor, a prompt checkup protects your health and creates a clear record of what happened to your body. Delays in treatment can raise doubts later about how serious the injuries really were. The second step is gathering evidence at the scene when it is safe to do so. Photos of the vehicles, the road, traffic signals, and any visible injuries can be useful. Contact details from witnesses can also help confirm what happened. The third step is keeping careful records. Save every medical bill, receipt, and note about missed work. Write down how the injuries affect daily life, from trouble sleeping to difficulty with simple tasks. These details help show the full impact of the crash. The fourth step is being careful with insurance conversations. It is wise to avoid guessing about fault, downplaying pain, or agreeing to a recorded statement before understanding your rights. Why Accountability Makes Roads Safer for Everyone Holding negligent drivers responsible is not only about one person's recovery. It also sends a message that careless behavior has consequences. When drivers and companies know they will be held accountable, they have a stronger reason to act with care. Commercial fleets, delivery services, and trucking companies are a good example. When their drivers cause harm, fair claims push these businesses to improve training, set safer schedules, and maintain their vehicles properly. Each step toward accountability can help prevent the next crash. Communities also benefit when people speak up. Reports of dangerous intersections, poor road design, and repeated crashes in the same area can lead to safety improvements. Individual cases often shine a light on wider problems that need attention. Fairness Should Never Depend on Who Has More Power Equal justice on the road means that every injured person, regardless of income or background, has a fair chance to be made whole. It means negligent drivers answer for the harm they cause, and insurers pay what is truly owed rather than what is easiest for them. No one plans for a crash, but everyone can prepare to respond wisely if one happens. By seeking medical care, keeping strong records, staying careful in insurance talks, and getting the right support, ordinary people can protect their rights. When individuals stand up for fair treatment, they help build a system that serves all drivers, not just the most powerful players.

articles.title: Los Angeles Rams
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Los Angeles Rams entered 2026 with the kind of roster that usually inspires championship conversations. Matthew Stafford remained at quarterback, Sean McVay was directing the offense, and the team had added considerable defensive star power. Expectations were understandably high. Six games later, the picture looked different. Los Angeles held a 2-4 record following an 18-16 defeat to Arizona on October 18, sitting fourth in the NFC West. That difficult opening hasn't made the Rams any less interesting. Their season now presents a fascinating question: can a talented collection of established stars overcome inconsistent performances and rediscover its winning formula? Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay: A Partnership Under Pressure Stafford and McVay have experienced the highest levels of NFL success together. Their partnership delivered a Super Bowl championship following the 2021 season, establishing a reputation for ambitious passing plays and sophisticated offensive preparation. Their challenge in 2026 involves producing those performances consistently. Against Buffalo on October 12, Stafford threw for 383 yards and three touchdowns. Los Angeles scored 34 points but still lost 37-34 in overtime, demonstrating how productive offense doesn't always translate into victory. McVay subsequently acknowledged regretting a conservative third-down play call that preceded a blocked 48-yard field goal attempt. Such moments carry considerable weight when margins are narrow. The Arizona game produced the opposite offensive problem. Los Angeles managed just 16 points against a divisional opponent that didn't score a touchdown. Stafford's experience and McVay's creativity remain significant strengths. Turning them into reliable production, particularly during crucial possessions, will shape the Rams' remaining season. Puka Nacua and Davante Adams: An Offense Built for Big Plays Few receiving combinations attract attention quite like Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. Their contrasting strengths give Stafford different ways to attack opposing defenses. Nacua thrives on physical catches, yards after contact, and making difficult receptions in traffic. His performance against Buffalo was remarkable: 17 receptions for 138 yards and a touchdown. Adams brings elite route-running experience and an ability to create separation through subtle changes of direction. Against the New York Giants on September 21, he caught eight passes for 195 yards and two touchdowns as Los Angeles secured a 28-6 victory. Nacua missed that game with a hip injury, making Adams' contribution particularly valuable. The Rams also possess rushing options through Kyren Williams and Blake Corum. An effective ground game can prevent defenses from concentrating exclusively on Stafford's receivers. The challenge involves bringing these elements together. Spectacular individual performances are entertaining, but sustainable offensive success requires protection, balanced play-calling, and consistent execution. Defensive Star Power: Can the Rams Deliver Consistently? Los Angeles entered 2026 with considerable defensive ambition. Aaron Donald returned from retirement, while Myles Garrett joined a unit already featuring talented younger contributors. Donald remains a familiar figure to Rams supporters. His ability to disrupt blocking assignments from the defensive interior can influence plays even without recording a sack. Garrett's availability has been a different story. A knee injury required surgery in September, and McVay confirmed on October 13 that the team wouldn’t open his 21-day practice window that week. Cornerback Trent McDuffie has also faced injury concerns, including a groin problem before the Arizona game. Despite those challenges, the defense produced a respectable performance against Arizona, preventing the Cardinals from scoring a touchdown. McVay acknowledged the unit's contribution afterward. The Rams nevertheless lost, reinforcing the importance of complementary performances across all three phases of the game. A Difficult Beginning Has Created Genuine Drama The Rams' first six games produced victories over the Giants and Eagles, alongside defeats against San Francisco, Denver, Buffalo, and Arizona. Their 2-4 start contrasted sharply with preseason expectations. Several losses have been especially frustrating because opportunities remained available late. Against Arizona, Los Angeles rallied to take a 16-15 lead before Chad Ryland converted a 43-yard field goal to secure an 18-16 Cardinals victory. Special teams complications added another layer of difficulty. Kicker Blake Grupe suffered an injury during the contest, leaving punter Ethan Evans handling placekicking responsibilities. These setbacks aren't evidence that the Rams lack talent. They do indicate that mistakes, injuries, and questionable decisions can undermine even well-equipped teams. Fans following the Los Angeles Rams odds can compare available team markets with recent results, injury developments, and upcoming opponents. Those markets reflect changing expectations rather than guarantees about future performances. NFC West Rivalries and a Demanding Schedule Ahead The Rams' remaining calendar offers numerous opportunities to assess their progress. Following their October 25 trip to Las Vegas, Los Angeles hosts the Chargers on November 1 before visiting Washington and Arizona in consecutive weeks. A bye follows in Week 11. Later assignments include Green Bay on November 25 and Kansas City on December 3. The Rams then travel to San Francisco on December 13, followed by a Christmas Day meeting with Seattle. Those divisional contests could become especially significant. Los Angeles already lost its opening meeting with the 49ers and suffered another NFC West defeat against Arizona. Winning subsequent rivalry games would improve its divisional record while potentially influencing postseason tiebreakers. The Chargers matchup adds local intrigue because both franchises share SoFi Stadium. Their different circumstances make the meeting an opportunity for Los Angeles to reestablish momentum. A difficult schedule isn't necessarily a disadvantage. Strong performances against respected opponents can change perceptions quickly, although the Rams must first correct the problems evident during their opening games. What Will Determine the Rams' Season? Consistency will matter more than reputation. Stafford and McVay need efficient offensive drives, while Nacua, Adams, and the rushing attack must contribute without relying on isolated spectacular plays. Defensive health presents another consideration. Fans following the latest team research and analysis can monitor injury developments, including Garrett's availability. Any return must follow medical clearance rather than expectations. Special teams execution also deserves attention after the Arizona setback. Close games frequently turn on details that receive less attention than passing yards or touchdowns. The Rams still have opportunities to improve, although their results must eventually justify the talent assembled. Why the Rams Remain Worth Watching Los Angeles possesses familiar stars, ambitious coaching, and an increasingly urgent need to perform. That combination creates uncertainty, even when individual players deliver impressive performances. The coming months will determine whether the Rams recover or continue struggling. Either way, their contrasting strengths and weaknesses make this one of the NFL's more intriguing stories in 2026.

articles.title: GPT-6 Astra and Jobs
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A demonstration ends with a completed spreadsheet or a working piece of software. The discussion immediately moves to how many people will lose their jobs. Concern about GPT-6 Astra and jobs deserves a more careful answer than that leap allows: which work has been demonstrated, under what conditions, and what would have to change before an employer could rely on it? There are several decisions between completing a task and eliminating a position. An organisation must adopt the system, connect it to its work, deal with its failures and decide how to use any resulting capacity. Workers have a stake in every one of those decisions. What does a GPT-6 Astra jobs claim actually cover? OpenAI presents GPT-6 Astra as a model for demanding work, including coding, computer use, research and document creation. Those capabilities are relevant to employment. They are not a count of positions that employers have removed because of the model. A job usually combines activities that differ considerably in their difficulty, frequency and consequences. Drafting a routine report is one activity. Finding out why two departments supplied conflicting figures is another. Deciding who may approve the corrected report adds a further responsibility. Suppose an office is considering an assistant that turns incoming requests into draft responses. A convincing demonstration might show a clear message arriving and a suitable reply appearing. The workplace still needs to handle incomplete messages, unusual cases, incorrect account details and people who cannot use the standard process. The relevant question is whether the system reduces the work across that whole process. If staff spend the saved drafting time checking records and correcting mistakes, the initial demonstration has described only part of the change. If the system also handles many routine cases reliably, that improvement deserves to be measured rather than assumed. Neither possibility tells us, by itself, what will happen to staffing. Managers might clear a backlog, expand a service, change hiring plans or reduce positions. A technical capability influences those choices without making them inevitable. Exposure is not a count of lost jobs The International Labour Organization's 2025 update on generative AI and jobs assesses occupational exposure through the tasks within occupations. It draws on task information, expert input and AI-assisted assessment. Its figures describe potential exposure to the technology, not an observed total of people who have lost work. The ILO also emphasises that continued human involvement makes transformation a more likely outcome than complete replacement for many jobs. That conclusion concerns a broad assessment of generative AI. It is not a study of employment changes caused specifically by Astra, and should not be presented as one. This distinction cuts both ways. Exposure is not proof that a position will disappear. It is also not a guarantee that the person holding it will be protected. A job can remain while its duties, workload or entry requirements change substantially. Read claims about employment with their time period attached. A forecast describes a possible future under stated assumptions. An employer announcement describes an intention. Recorded reductions describe something that happened, but attributing them to one technology requires more evidence about the decision and other changes in the business. The denominator matters as well. Tasks, working hours, vacancies and employed people are different units. A claim that a tool can assist with several tasks cannot be turned into an equivalent percentage of employees without showing the steps in between. For public discussion, a useful description names the unit, the place and the period. It also says whether the result is modelled, reported by an employer or observed in employment data. Readers should not have to reconstruct those distinctions from a footnote after a dramatic headline. A workplace trial should include the work around the output Before relying on a new system, document the existing process with the people who perform it. Include the awkward cases that rarely appear in demonstrations: information arriving late, a request changing halfway through, or an error that becomes visible only after another team acts on it. A comparison involving Claude Opus 5.5 or another model should use the same cases and acceptance rules. Otherwise the exercise can become a contest between selected examples, while leaving the workplace's real constraints unexplored. Assess a completed task after the necessary review, not merely when text first appears on screen. Record what had to be corrected, who did the correction and whether a later problem required the task to be reopened. That produces a fuller account of the work a system saves or creates. Keep responsibility explicit. If an automated draft gives someone the wrong instruction, there should be a known route for correcting it and reaching a person who can resolve the case. A workflow that leaves staff responsible while hiding the information they need to investigate is poorly designed, however impressive its demonstrations look. Who gets a say in the change? Workers should be involved before a pilot becomes a new performance target. They can identify missing steps and exceptions that a manager or supplier may not see. Give them a way to report failures without making the report itself evidence of poor performance. The terms of the trial should also explain how employee activity will be recorded, who can examine those records and what conclusions may be drawn from them. A tool introduced to help draft a document should not quietly become an unexplained score of the person using it. Ask what happens if the trial works. Will employees receive time to learn changed duties? Will a shorter routine process reduce an existing backlog, or simply produce a higher daily target? These are decisions about how work is organised. They deserve an answer even when the software performs well. Debate about GPT-6 Astra and jobs becomes more useful when it reaches those decisions. Ask for evidence of the actual task, the surrounding review and the resulting change in work. Then ask who helped decide what to do with that change. A finished demo cannot answer that last question. The workplace still needs to handle incomplete messages, unusual cases, incorrect account details and people who cannot use the standard process. The relevant question is whether the system reduces the work across that whole process. If staff spend the saved drafting time checking records and correcting mistakes, the initial demonstration has described only part of the change. If the system also handles many routine cases reliably, that improvement deserves to be measured rather than assumed. Neither possibility tells us, by itself, what will happen to staffing. Managers might clear a backlog, expand a service, change hiring plans or reduce positions. A technical capability influences those choices without making them inevitable. Exposure is not a count of lost jobs The International Labour Organization's 2025 update on generative AI and jobs assesses occupational exposure through the tasks within occupations. It draws on task information, expert input and AI-assisted assessment. Its figures describe potential exposure to the technology, not an observed total of people who have lost work. The ILO also emphasises that continued human involvement makes transformation a more likely outcome than complete replacement for many jobs. That conclusion concerns a broad assessment of generative AI. It is not a study of employment changes caused specifically by Astra, and should not be presented as one. This distinction cuts both ways. Exposure is not proof that a position will disappear. It is also not a guarantee that the person holding it will be protected. A job can remain while its duties, workload or entry requirements change substantially. Read claims about employment with their time period attached. A forecast describes a possible future under stated assumptions. An employer announcement describes an intention. Recorded reductions describe something that happened, but attributing them to one technology requires more evidence about the decision and other changes in the business. The denominator matters as well. Tasks, working hours, vacancies and employed people are different units. A claim that a tool can assist with several tasks cannot be turned into an equivalent percentage of employees without showing the steps in between. For public discussion, a useful description names the unit, the place and the period. It also says whether the result is modelled, reported by an employer or observed in employment data. Readers should not have to reconstruct those distinctions from a footnote after a dramatic headline. A workplace trial should include the work around the output Before relying on a new system, document the existing process with the people who perform it. Include the awkward cases that rarely appear in demonstrations: information arriving late, a request changing halfway through, or an error that becomes visible only after another team acts on it. A comparison involving Claude Opus 5.5 or another model should use the same cases and acceptance rules. Otherwise the exercise can become a contest between selected examples, while leaving the workplace's real constraints unexplored. Assess a completed task after the necessary review, not merely when text first appears on screen. Record what had to be corrected, who did the correction and whether a later problem required the task to be reopened. That produces a fuller account of the work a system saves or creates. Keep responsibility explicit. If an automated draft gives someone the wrong instruction, there should be a known route for correcting it and reaching a person who can resolve the case. A workflow that leaves staff responsible while hiding the information they need to investigate is poorly designed, however impressive its demonstrations look. Who gets a say in the change? Workers should be involved before a pilot becomes a new performance target. They can identify missing steps and exceptions that a manager or supplier may not see. Give them a way to report failures without making the report itself evidence of poor performance. The terms of the trial should also explain how employee activity will be recorded, who can examine those records and what conclusions may be drawn from them. A tool introduced to help draft a document should not quietly become an unexplained score of the person using it. Ask what happens if the trial works. Will employees receive time to learn changed duties? Will a shorter routine process reduce an existing backlog, or simply produce a higher daily target? These are decisions about how work is organised. They deserve an answer even when the software performs well. Debate about GPT-6 Astra and jobs becomes more useful when it reaches those decisions. Ask for evidence of the actual task, the surrounding review and the resulting change in work. Then ask who helped decide what to do with that change. A finished demo cannot answer that last question.
